# Lesson 01 — Board representation and validation: Theory

**Engineering** · *Stage 0: Classical foundations*
## The idea

Representation is not clerical work. The form you choose decides which
operations are cheap, and cheap operations are the ones you will actually use.

Sudoku's state is 81 variables over the domain {1..9}, plus a marker for
"undecided". Three encodings compete:

- **Dense integer** — one number per cell, 0 for empty. Compact, but it implies
  an ordering: 7 is not "greater than" 3 in any meaningful sense, and a model
  fed raw digits as floats will assume otherwise.
- **One-hot** — nine (or ten) booleans per cell. No false ordering, larger.
- **Bitmask** — a 9-bit integer per cell holding the *set* of remaining
  possibilities. This is one-hot's dual and it is what a solver wants, because
  set intersection is `&` and set removal is `& ~`.

This repo uses dense integers for storage and interchange, and switches to
bitmasks the moment reasoning starts (Lesson 03). Stage 2 switches to one-hot
for models. Same state, three encodings, each earning its place.

## Formally

A board is a function `b: C -> {0, 1, ..., 9}` where `C` is the 81 cells and 0
means undecided. A *completion* of `b` is a total function
`s: C -> {1..9}` agreeing with `b` on every cell where `b` is nonzero.

Three predicates, deliberately distinguished:

- `complete(b)` iff `b(c) != 0` for all `c`
- `consistent(b)` iff no two cells sharing a unit have the same nonzero value
- `solved(b)` iff `complete(b) and consistent(b)`

`consistent` is a *local* property: checkable in O(n) by scanning units.
`solved` is local too. But "does a consistent partial board have a completion?"
is not local at all — it is the NP-complete question (Yato & Seta, 2003, for
the generalised n^2 x n^2 case), and no amount of validation code answers it.
Only search does.

## Why it matters here

Every failure mode you will meet in Stage 2 is a confusion between these three
predicates. A neural network that outputs a complete but inconsistent grid has
not "nearly solved" anything. A model scoring 95% cell accuracy is producing
boards that are complete, wrong, and usually inconsistent — and `is_solved`
will tell you so in one call.

The flat-versus-2D choice matters for a subtler reason. `numpy`'s `reshape`
returns a *view* when the memory layout permits, so keeping the flat form
canonical costs nothing and gains you free 2D access. Choosing 9x9 as canonical
would make the 81-token sequence view in Lesson 16 the awkward one instead.

## Pitfalls

- Treating a view as a copy. `to_grid(b)[0, 0] = 5` mutates `b`.
- Assuming consistent implies solvable. It does not.
- Feeding raw digits to a network as floats. You have asserted 9 > 8 > 7,
  which is false in this domain, and the model will waste capacity unlearning it.

## Further reading

- Yato & Seta (2003), *Complexity and completeness of finding another solution
  and its application to puzzles* — the NP-completeness result.
- Felgenhauer & Jarvis (2005) counted the valid grids:
  6,670,903,752,021,072,936,960, of which 5,472,730,538 are essentially
  distinct once symmetry is quotiented out.

# Lesson 02 — Units, peers, and the constraint graph: Theory

**Classical AI** · *Stage 0: Classical foundations*
## The idea

Before you can reason about a puzzle you must know its structure, and sudoku's
structure is a graph. Each cell is a vertex; two vertices are adjacent when
their cells may not hold the same digit. Solving the puzzle is then exactly
**graph colouring**: assign one of 9 colours to every vertex so that no edge
joins two vertices of the same colour, respecting the pre-coloured vertices.

That reframing is worth more than it first appears. It tells you immediately
that sudoku is an instance of a well-studied NP-complete problem, that
everything known about colouring heuristics applies, and — in Stage 3 — that
the graph itself is the natural computation structure for a neural network.

## Formally

Let `C` be the 81 cells. A **unit** is a subset `U` of `C` with `|U| = 9`
carrying an all-different constraint. There are 27: nine rows, nine columns,
nine boxes.

The **peers** of a cell `c` are `P(c) = (union of units containing c) \ {c}`.

Every cell lies in exactly three units, so a naive count gives 3 x 8 = 24
peers. But a cell's box shares two cells with its row and two with its column,
and those four are double-counted:

    |P(c)| = 8 + 8 + 8 - 2 - 2 = 20

The graph `G = (C, E)` with `E = {{a, b} : b in P(a)}` is therefore
**20-regular** on 81 vertices, giving

    |E| = (81 x 20) / 2 = 810

edges. The division by two is the whole content of the "why 810 and not 1620"
question: adjacency is symmetric, and an undirected edge should be counted once.

The graph has diameter 2 — any two cells are at most two hops apart — which is
a fact you will need in Lesson 22 when choosing how many message-passing rounds
a GNN needs.

## Why it matters here

Three payoffs, one per stage:

- **Stage 0.** Peers are read in the innermost loop of every propagator. They
  are precomputed once at import and frozen.
- **Stage 2.** "Which cells does this cell depend on?" is exactly the attention
  mask in Lesson 16. You can *impose* the peer structure on attention rather
  than hoping the model discovers it.
- **Stage 3.** The graph is the message-passing topology for the GNN.

## Pitfalls

- Recomputing peers inside a loop. It is a constant; treat it as one.
- Forgetting that a cell's box overlaps its row and column — the source of the
  common wrong answer of 24 peers.
- Assuming the graph is complete within a unit *and* nothing else. It is the
  union of 27 cliques of size 9, which is not the same as a random 20-regular
  graph, and its block structure is visible in the adjacency matrix.

## Further reading

- Russell & Norvig, *AIML*, chapter 6, for the general CSP framing.
- Any graph-colouring reference: sudoku is the pre-coloured case of
  9-colouring, sometimes called *list colouring*.

# Lesson 03 — Constraint propagation: naked and hidden singles: Theory

**Classical AI** · *Stage 0: Classical foundations*
## The idea

Search is expensive; inference is cheap. Before guessing anything, squeeze out
every conclusion that follows with certainty from what you already know. That
is constraint propagation, and on sudoku it is astonishingly effective — most
published "easy" and "medium" puzzles fall to it without a single guess.

Two rules do nearly all the work:

**Naked single.** If a cell has exactly one candidate left, it must take it.
This is reasoning *about a cell*: "nothing else fits here."

**Hidden single.** If, within a unit, a digit has exactly one cell that can
still host it, it goes there — even if that cell has five other candidates.
This is reasoning *about a digit*: "it has to go somewhere, and there is only
one place left."

These feel similar and are not. The first looks at one cell's domain. The
second looks across nine cells at once, and that difference is exactly the gap
between arc consistency and something stronger (Lesson 04).

## Formally

Maintain a domain `D(c) subset {1..9}` per cell.

    Naked single:  |D(c)| = 1, D(c) = {v}  =>  for all p in P(c): D(p) <- D(p) \ {v}
    Hidden single: exists unit U, digit v, unique c in U with v in D(c)
                   =>  D(c) <- {v}

Both are **monotone**: domains only shrink. So iterating to a fixpoint
terminates, and the fixpoint is unique regardless of application order (the
rules form a closure operator). If any `D(c)` becomes empty, the board is
unsolvable — that is the contradiction signal search relies on.

The bitmask implementation makes each operation a single machine instruction:

    intersection    a & b
    removal         a & ~(1 << (v - 1))
    is singleton    a.bit_count() == 1
    the digit       a.bit_length()

## Why it matters here

This is the baseline every neural network in Stage 2 is competing against, and
it is a *very* strong baseline: exact, instant, and total. Any model that
solves fewer puzzles than plain propagation has learned nothing worth having.

It is also the thing iterative decoding (Lesson 17) turns out to imitate. When
you fill the most confident cell and re-run the model, you have reinvented
naked singles with a learned confidence function in place of a proof. Noticing
that correspondence is the intellectual centre of this repo.

## Pitfalls

- Stopping after one pass. Propagation must run to a fixpoint; one assignment
  unlocks others.
- Forgetting that a fixpoint is not a solution. Propagation can terminate with
  every domain non-singleton and no contradiction. That is where search starts.
- Implementing hidden singles without re-running naked singles afterwards. Each
  rule feeds the other.

## Further reading

- Peter Norvig, *Solving Every Sudoku Puzzle* — the classic essay. His
  `assign`/`eliminate` pair fuses both rules into one mutually recursive
  routine; worth reading after you have implemented them separately.

# Lesson 04 — Arc consistency (AC-3), and its limits: Theory

**Classical AI** · *Stage 0: Classical foundations*
## The idea

Arc consistency is the standard workhorse of constraint programming, and this
lesson is about discovering that on sudoku, as usually formulated, it is
disappointingly weak — and understanding exactly why, because the reason is
general and important.

The catch is **decomposition**. A unit's "all nine digits differ" is one
constraint over nine variables. Encoding it as 36 pairwise `!=` constraints
looks equivalent — the same solutions satisfy both — but it is strictly weaker
*for propagation*. Information that lives in the constraint as a whole is
destroyed by splitting it up.

## Formally

An arc `(Xi, Xj)` is **arc consistent** if for every value `x` in `D(Xi)` there
exists some `y` in `D(Xj)` with `(x, y)` satisfying the constraint. AC-3
repeatedly calls `Revise(Xi, Xj)`, removing unsupported values, re-queueing
`(Xk, Xi)` for every other neighbour `Xk` when `D(Xi)` changes. It runs in
`O(e d^3)` for `e` arcs and domain size `d`.

Now specialise to `Xi != Xj`. A value `x` in `D(Xi)` is unsupported iff *every*
`y` in `D(Xj)` equals `x` — which requires `D(Xj) = {x}`. So:

    Revise prunes anything  <=>  |D(Xj)| = 1

and the only pruning it performs is removing that singleton value from the
neighbour. **That is precisely the naked-single rule.** AC-3 over the binary
decomposition and naked-single propagation compute the identical fixpoint.
There is a test asserting it: `test_ac3_is_no_stronger_than_naked_singles`.

Hidden singles escape this because they are a statement about a set of nine
variables jointly. No binary constraint can express "digit 7 has only one home
left in this row."

The fix is a **global constraint**. Régin (1994) gave a filtering algorithm for
`AllDifferent` achieving generalised arc consistency by modelling the
variable-value relation as a bipartite graph and using matching theory: a value
survives iff it lies in some maximum matching. Hall's theorem gives the
intuition — if `k` variables collectively have only `k` candidate values, no
other variable in that unit may use any of them.

## Why it matters here

This is the single most transferable idea in Stage 0. "Decomposing a global
constraint into binary ones loses propagation strength" explains why industrial
solvers invest so heavily in global constraints, and it is why CP-SAT
(Lesson 37) will beat everything you write by hand.

It also sets up Stage 3's premise. If stronger inference means less search,
then a *learned* inference rule — one that is fast but not sound — might buy
the same reduction, provided search remains available to catch its mistakes.

## Pitfalls

- Concluding "AC-3 is useless." It is not; it is exactly as strong as naked
  singles, which is already most of the way. The lesson is about the ceiling.
- Believing equivalent *solution sets* implies equivalent *propagation*. This is
  the core misconception the lesson exists to break.

## Further reading

- Régin (1994), *A filtering algorithm for constraints of difference in CSPs*.
- Mackworth (1977) for AC-3 itself.
- Hall's marriage theorem, for why matching is the right tool.

# Lesson 05 — Backtracking search and its heuristics: Theory

**Classical AI** · *Stage 0: Classical foundations*
## The idea

When inference runs out, guess — but guess in the order that hurts least, and
be ready to take it back. Backtracking search is depth-first traversal of the
assignment tree with immediate abandonment of any branch proven inconsistent.

Its cost is dominated not by the algorithm but by two orderings:

- **Which variable to branch on** — and here the counterintuitive answer is to
  pick the *most constrained* one. This is the **fail-first principle**: if a
  branch is doomed, you want to find out at depth 2, not depth 40. MRV picks
  the cell with the fewest remaining candidates.
- **Which value to try first** — and here the principle inverts. You want the
  value most likely to *succeed*, so LCV picks the value that removes the
  fewest candidates from peers.

Fail-first on variables, succeed-first on values. They are not contradictory:
you must eventually examine every variable, so you want the cheapest refutation
first; but you only need one value to work, so you want the likeliest first.

## Formally

    function BACKTRACK(assignment, csp):
        if assignment is complete: return assignment
        var <- SELECT-UNASSIGNED-VARIABLE(csp, assignment)
        for value in ORDER-DOMAIN-VALUES(var, assignment, csp):
            if value is consistent with assignment:
                add {var = value} to assignment
                inferences <- INFERENCE(csp, var, value)
                if inferences != failure:
                    result <- BACKTRACK(assignment, csp)
                    if result != failure: return result
            remove {var = value} and inferences
        return failure

`INFERENCE` is where Lesson 03 plugs in. Without it, search on a hard sudoku
explores millions of nodes. With propagation at every node, the same puzzle
typically needs a handful — this repo's hard test case needs **3**.

Heuristics, in the order they pay off:

- **MRV** — fewest remaining values. Usually the single largest win.
- **Degree** — most constraints on unassigned variables. A tie-breaker for MRV.
- **LCV** — least constraining value. Cheaper wins; costs work to compute.
- **Forward checking / full propagation** — the biggest win of all, and the
  reason the numbers above are so small.

## Why it matters here

Node count is the metric this whole repo measures search by, and this is the
lesson where you learn to read it. Wall-clock time is a trap: it conflates
algorithmic quality with Python overhead, and in Stage 3 — where each node may
involve a neural network forward pass — it will actively mislead you.

The `select_var` and `order_values` hooks in
`src/gridmind/solvers/backtracking.py` exist so that Lesson 21 can replace MRV
with a learned policy and compare on exactly this axis.

## Pitfalls

- Measuring seconds instead of nodes when comparing heuristics.
- Reporting the mean node count. The distribution is heavy-tailed; use the
  median and report the max separately.
- Forgetting to undo inferences on backtrack. This repo copies the domain list
  per branch — simple and correct. A trail-based undo is faster and is a fine
  optimisation exercise.

## Further reading

- Haralick & Elliott (1980) for fail-first.
- Russell & Norvig chapter 6.3 for the heuristic zoo.

# Lesson 06 — Exact cover: Algorithm X and dancing links: Theory

**Classical AI** · *Stage 0: Classical foundations*
## The idea

Sometimes the fastest route to a solution is to stop solving the problem you
were given and solve a different one that happens to be equivalent. Sudoku is
an instance of **exact cover**, and exact cover has a beautiful algorithm.

Exact cover: given a 0/1 matrix, select a subset of rows such that every column
contains exactly one 1 among the selected rows. Knuth's **Algorithm X** solves
it by recursive column-choice and row-selection; **Dancing Links (DLX)** is the
implementation trick that makes it fast.

## Formally

Encode sudoku as a matrix with **729 rows** and **324 columns**.

Rows: one per (cell, digit) pair — "cell 40 holds a 7". 81 x 9 = 729.

Columns: four constraint families, 81 each:

1. *Cell* — cell `c` is filled. (81)
2. *Row-digit* — row `r` contains digit `d`. (81)
3. *Column-digit* — column `k` contains digit `d`. (81)
4. *Box-digit* — box `b` contains digit `d`. (81)

Total 324. Each row has exactly four 1s, one per family. A set of rows covering
every column exactly once is precisely a valid completed grid. Givens are
handled by pre-selecting their rows.

**Dancing links** is the observation that in a circular doubly-linked list,

    x.left.right <- x.right ;  x.right.left <- x.left      (remove x)
    x.left.right <- x ;        x.right.left <- x           (restore x)

removal is undone by an operation of identical cost, because `x` still holds
its own pointers. Backtracking therefore costs nothing extra — no copying, no
trail. The matrix is stored as a sparse mesh of nodes linked in four
directions, and the search dances rows and columns in and out of it.

Algorithm X's one heuristic: choose the column with the fewest remaining 1s.
That is MRV again, in different clothing.

## Why it matters here

Two lessons, one practical and one conceptual.

Practically, DLX will beat your backtracking solver, and seeing that is worth
the implementation effort.

Conceptually: *reformulation is a technique*. The same instinct — "is this
secretly a problem I already know how to solve?" — reappears in Lesson 36 (as
SAT) and Lesson 38 (rostering as a CSP). Recognising the shape of a problem is
often worth more than optimising the obvious approach.

## Pitfalls

- Deriving 324 as anything other than 4 x 81. Work out each family separately.
- Writing DLX first. Implement Algorithm X with plain Python sets, get it
  correct, *then* optimise. Debugging a broken linked-list mesh is unpleasant.
- Forgetting that removal order and restoration order must mirror each other
  exactly.

## Further reading

- Knuth (2000), *Dancing Links*. Short, clear, and genuinely enjoyable.

# Lesson 07 — Puzzle generation and uniqueness: Theory

**Classical AI** · *Stage 0: Classical foundations*
## The idea

Generation is the inverse problem, and it is harder than solving. You need
puzzles that are **well-formed**: exactly one solution. Not zero, and — the
part people forget — not two.

The standard method is *dig from a solution*: build a complete valid grid, then
remove clues one at a time, keeping a removal only if the puzzle still has a
unique solution.

## Formally

    1. Fill an empty grid using the solver with randomised value ordering.
    2. Shuffle the 81 cells.
    3. For each cell: tentatively clear it. If count_solutions(puzzle, 2) != 1,
       put it back.

The uniqueness test is the expensive step, so note what makes it affordable:
you never count all solutions, you stop at **two**. Establishing "more than
one exists" needs only a second witness, and the solver finds one fast or not
at all.

Facts worth knowing:

- **17 is the minimum.** McGuire, Tugemann and Civario (2012) proved by
  exhaustive computer search that no 16-clue puzzle has a unique solution.
  Random digging essentially never reaches 17; low 20s is a realistic floor.
- **Digging order matters.** Different shuffles give different clue counts from
  the same completed grid.
- **Symmetry costs clues.** Removing cells in 180-degree pairs — the convention
  in published puzzles — forces you to keep a cell whenever its partner is
  needed, so symmetric puzzles bottom out higher.

## Why it matters here

This module is the reason the entire curriculum runs offline. It is an
unlimited, self-contained, correctly-labelled data source. Most ML side
projects die at data collection; here it is a loop.

Uniqueness is not pedantry — it is **label correctness**. If a puzzle has two
solutions and you train against one of them, you punish the network for
producing the other, which is equally valid. You are teaching it noise. Every
supervised label in Stages 2 through 5 depends on this check.

## Pitfalls

- Skipping the uniqueness check because the puzzle "looks fine". Corrupt labels
  are silent; you will see it as an accuracy ceiling you cannot explain.
- Treating clue count as difficulty. It correlates weakly. See Lesson 31.
- Generating with a fixed seed and then wondering why train and test look alike.

## Further reading

- McGuire, Tugemann & Civario (2012), *There is no 16-clue sudoku*.

# Lesson 08 — Benchmarking and difficulty proxies: Theory

**Engineering** · *Stage 0: Classical foundations*
## The idea

Every claim in the rest of this repo is a comparison, and a comparison is only
as good as its measurement protocol. This lesson builds that protocol before
there is anything interesting to measure — deliberately, because a harness
built after the fact is a harness built to flatter the result.

## Formally

Three principles.

**Measure the algorithm, not the language.** Node count is implementation- and
hardware-independent. Wall-clock time measures your Python, your CPU, and the
weather. Report nodes as primary, time as secondary, and never compare
heuristics on time alone.

**Use the median.** Search cost distributions are heavy-tailed: most puzzles
are trivial, a few are brutal. The mean is dragged around by the tail and is
unstable across samples. Report median for central tendency, max for the tail,
and plot the distribution on a log scale — where a heavy tail shows as a long
right shoulder rather than a spike.

**Stratify.** An aggregate accuracy over mixed difficulty is nearly
meaningless, because it silently reports the mix rather than the model. Always
break results down by clue count. `metrics.by_clue_count` does this, and it is
the table that reveals whether a Stage 2 model reasons or merely pattern-matches:
a memorising model looks fine at 40 clues and collapses below 25.

**Fix seeds.** Generation, augmentation, splitting, initialisation, shuffling.
An unreproducible number is an anecdote.

## Why it matters here

Stage 3 asks "did the learned heuristic help?" That question has no meaning
without this harness. Stage 2 asks "is this architecture better?" — same.

There is also a discipline point. Building measurement *first* means you cannot
tune the metric to the result. It is much easier to define "better" honestly
before you have a favourite.

## Pitfalls

- Comparing runs with different seeds and attributing the difference to your
  change.
- Quoting mean node counts. One pathological puzzle moves it by an order of
  magnitude.
- Reporting a single aggregate number. Stratify or the number is misleading.
- Benchmarking on the puzzles you developed against. Generate a fresh set.

## Further reading

- Any experimental-methods chapter in an empirical algorithms text; the
  conventions here are standard practice in the SAT and CP competition
  communities.

# Lesson 09 — Tensors, encoding, and the shape of the problem: Theory

**ML** · *Stage 1: Data*
## The idea

A model does not see a sudoku grid; it sees a tensor. How you build that tensor
encodes assumptions, and one of the obvious choices encodes a false one.

## Formally

Three candidate encodings for an 81-cell board:

**Integer.** Shape `(B, 81)`, values 0-9, fed as floats. Compact and *wrong*:
it asserts that the digits are ordered and evenly spaced, that 9 is "far from"
1 and "adjacent to" 8. In sudoku the digit labels are arbitrary — Lesson 10
shows you can permute all nine and the puzzle is unchanged. Any capacity the
model spends unlearning this ordering is wasted.

**One-hot.** Shape `(B, 81, 10)` — nine digits plus an empty marker — or
`(B, 10, 9, 9)` for convolutions. No spurious ordering. This is the honest
default and what most sudoku models use.

**Learned embedding.** Shape `(B, 81, d)` via `nn.Embedding(10, d)`. Equivalent
to one-hot followed by a linear layer, but lets the model choose `d`. Natural
for the transformer in Lesson 16.

You also need a **mask**: which cells were given. Givens are inputs, not
predictions, and scoring the model on reproducing them inflates accuracy for
free. A 40-clue puzzle is 49% given; a model that copies inputs and guesses the
rest already "scores" 40-something percent.

Shapes to keep straight:

    (B, 81)         integer board
    (B, 81, 10)     one-hot, sequence view      -> transformer
    (B, 10, 9, 9)   one-hot, image view         -> CNN
    (B, 81)         bool mask of given cells
    (B, 81)         integer targets, 1-9

## Why it matters here

Encoding is where domain knowledge enters a model most cheaply. You get to
choose what the network must learn and what it is simply told. Telling it that
digits are unordered costs nothing; making it discover that costs capacity and
data.

On this machine, note `torch.backends.mps.is_available()` is `True` — the Apple
GPU works. Move tensors and model to `mps` together, or you will meet a device
mismatch error.

## Pitfalls

- Feeding raw digits as floats. The single most common beginner error here.
- Forgetting the empty marker, so 0 becomes "digit zero".
- Losing the given-mask, then reporting inflated accuracy.
- Building tensors inside the training loop instead of the `Dataset`.

## Further reading

- PyTorch `Dataset` / `DataLoader` docs — the abstraction is worth learning
  properly once.

# Lesson 10 — Symmetry augmentation: Theory

**ML** · *Stage 1: Data*
## The idea

Sudoku has a large symmetry group: transformations that map valid grids to
valid grids and preserve the puzzle-solution relationship. Apply one to a
`(puzzle, solution)` pair and you get another perfectly valid pair, for free.

This is the best-case scenario for data augmentation — the transformations are
*exact*, not approximate. Unlike rotating a photograph, there is no risk of
producing something unrealistic. But "free data" is not the same as "free
information", and the difference matters.

## Formally

The group is generated by:

- **Digit relabelling** — any permutation of {1..9}: `9! = 362,880`
- **Row permutation within a band** — `3!` per band, three bands: `6^3`
- **Band permutation** — `3! = 6`
- **Column permutation within a stack** — `6^3`
- **Stack permutation** — `6`
- **Transposition** — `2`

Grid symmetries: `6^3 x 6 x 6^3 x 6 x 2 = 6^8 x 2 = 3,359,232`.
With relabelling: `3,359,232 x 362,880 = 1,218,998,108,160`.

Roughly 1.2 trillion variants of any single grid. Note what is *not* in the
group: arbitrary row permutations (they break boxes) and rotations other than
those expressible as transpose-plus-permutation.

The crucial caveat: these variants are not independent samples. They are the
orbit of one point under a group action. A model can in principle learn the
invariance and then treat all 1.2 trillion as the one puzzle they are. So
augmentation reduces overfitting to surface form; it does not add information
about the *distribution of puzzles*.

Which leads directly to the trap in Lesson 11: if augmented copies of one base
grid land on both sides of a train/test split, your test set contains
transformed copies of your training data, and your score is a memorisation
score.

## Why it matters here

Augmentation is one of the highest-leverage tools in applied ML and one of the
easiest to misuse. Sudoku makes both halves unusually legible: the transforms
are provably valid, and the leakage is provably catastrophic. You can measure
both effects exactly, which you cannot do with image augmentation.

## Pitfalls

- Transforming puzzle and solution with *different* random draws. The pair must
  stay consistent — test it.
- Permuting rows across band boundaries. Breaks the boxes; the result is not a
  valid sudoku.
- Splitting before grouping. See Lesson 11.
- Believing 1.2 trillion variants means 1.2 trillion training examples.

## Further reading

- Felgenhauer & Jarvis (2005) and Russell & Jarvis (2006) on counting grids and
  the essentially-distinct count of 5,472,730,538 under this group.

# Lesson 11 — Splits, grouping, and leakage: Theory

**ML** · *Stage 1: Data*
## The idea

The purpose of a validation set is to estimate performance on data the model
has not seen. Any path by which information about the test set reaches training
destroys that estimate — and the failure is silent. Your numbers get *better*,
which is precisely why it goes uncaught.

## Formally

The assumption behind a random split is that rows are independent. Augmentation
breaks it. If base grid `g` produces variants `g1..g8` and a random split puts
`g1..g6` in train and `g7, g8` in test, the test set is a relabelled,
row-permuted copy of training data. A model with enough capacity to invert the
symmetry — and they do — scores near-perfectly while having learned nothing
transferable.

The fix is a **grouped split**: assign a group id to every row (here, the base
grid index), split on *groups*, then take all rows of a group with it.

    groups     = unique(group_ids)
    shuffle(groups)
    train_g, val_g, test_g = partition(groups)
    train_idx  = rows whose group is in train_g          # etc.

`dataset.split_by_group` does this. `dataset.naive_split` deliberately does not,
so you can run both and measure the gap. That gap is the size of the lie, and
seeing it in your own numbers is worth more than being told about it.

Other leakage routes worth knowing, because they generalise past this repo:

- **Temporal leakage** — training on future data to predict the past.
- **Preprocessing leakage** — fitting a scaler or vocabulary on the full
  dataset before splitting.
- **Duplicate leakage** — the same record appearing twice under different ids.
- **Target leakage** — a feature computed from the label.

## Why it matters here

This is the most transferable lesson in the repo. Leakage is the single most
common way real ML projects report results they cannot reproduce in production,
and it is nearly always structural rather than a coding bug: the split did not
respect a grouping that existed in the data.

The habit to build: before splitting anything, ask *what is the unit of
independence here?* Rarely the row. Often a user, a patient, a document, a
session — or a base grid.

## Pitfalls

- Splitting after augmenting. Always split first, then augment each side.
- Grouping on the wrong key.
- Fitting normalisation statistics before the split.
- Trusting a validation number that improved suspiciously fast.

## Further reading

- Kaufman et al. (2012), *Leakage in data mining*.
- scikit-learn's `GroupKFold` documentation.

# Lesson 12 — A training loop, written by hand: Theory

**ML** · *Stage 2: Supervised deep learning*
## The idea

A training loop is four steps in a cycle: run the model forward, measure how
wrong it was, push that error backwards to get gradients, nudge the parameters.
Everything else a framework offers -- schedulers, callbacks, mixed precision,
distributed training -- is instrumentation around those four lines.

Write it by hand once and the mystery goes away permanently.

## Formally

You are minimising an average loss over the dataset:

    L(theta) = (1/N) * sum_i loss(f_theta(x_i), y_i)

by repeatedly stepping downhill:

    theta <- theta - eta * grad L(theta)

Stochastic gradient descent estimates that gradient from a mini-batch rather
than the whole dataset. The estimate is noisy, and the noise is useful -- it is
part of why SGD generalises.

Backpropagation is reverse-mode automatic differentiation: the chain rule,
applied from the loss backwards, reusing intermediate results. It costs roughly
twice a forward pass, regardless of how many parameters there are. That
asymmetry is the reason deep learning is practical at all.

In PyTorch the cycle is:

    optimizer.zero_grad()      # gradients accumulate by default
    output = model(x)
    loss = criterion(output, y)
    loss.backward()            # populates .grad on every parameter
    optimizer.step()           # applies the update

## Why it matters here

Sudoku output is 81 cells, each a 9-way classification. The natural loss is
cross-entropy per cell, averaged over the cells you actually asked the model to
predict -- the empty ones. Givens are inputs; scoring the model on copying them
inflates the number for free (Lesson 18).

The single most valuable habit in this lesson is the **overfit-one-batch smoke
test**. Take eight puzzles and train until the model reproduces them almost
perfectly. A correct loop can always do this. If yours cannot, the bug is in
the loop -- the loss, the masking, or the target indexing -- and no amount of
training on the full dataset will reveal it. Debug on eight examples, not
eighty thousand.

## Pitfalls

- Forgetting `zero_grad()`. Gradients accumulate, so you silently train on the
  sum of every batch so far and the loss goes strange rather than erroring.
- Evaluating without `torch.no_grad()`. It still works, but it builds a graph
  you never use and can exhaust memory.
- Targets off by one. Cross-entropy wants classes `0..8`, so digit `d` becomes
  class `d - 1`. Get this wrong and the model learns a permuted digit map that
  looks almost plausible.
- Forgetting `model.train()` / `model.eval()`. It matters the moment you add
  dropout or batch norm.
- Reporting cell accuracy and calling it success. See Lesson 08.

## Further reading

- Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville, *Deep Learning*, chapters 6 and 8.
- PyTorch's own 60-minute blitz -- worth doing once even if it feels basic.

# Lesson 13 — Autograd, optimizers, and schedules: Theory

**ML** · *Stage 2: Supervised deep learning*
## The idea

Autograd records the operations you perform on tensors, building a directed
acyclic graph. `backward()` walks that graph in reverse applying the chain
rule. You never write a derivative; you write the forward computation and get
the backward one free.

Optimisers differ only in what they do with the gradients once they arrive.

## Formally

**SGD** takes the gradient at face value:

    theta <- theta - eta * g

**Momentum** accumulates an exponentially-weighted average of past gradients,
which damps oscillation across narrow valleys:

    v <- mu * v + g ;  theta <- theta - eta * v

**Adam** (Kingma & Ba, 2014) keeps running estimates of both the first and
second moments of the gradient and scales each parameter's step by its own
recent gradient magnitude:

    m <- b1*m + (1-b1)*g
    v <- b2*v + (1-b2)*g^2
    theta <- theta - eta * m_hat / (sqrt(v_hat) + eps)

This is why Adam is forgiving about learning rate: parameters with large
gradients get small steps automatically. **AdamW** (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2017)
decouples weight decay from the adaptive scaling, which is what you usually
want.

**Learning rate is the hyperparameter that matters most.** Too high and the
loss diverges or goes NaN; too low and training crawls or settles in a poor
region. Schedules trade exploration for refinement: warmup avoids early
instability, cosine decay anneals smoothly to near zero.

**Gradient clipping** rescales the gradient when its norm exceeds a threshold.
It is a blunt instrument, and it converts a divergence into slow progress
rather than fixing the cause.

## Why it matters here

The models in this stage are small and the data is clean and unlimited, which
makes it an unusually good laboratory. You can sweep learning rates over three
orders of magnitude in minutes and watch the classic picture emerge: divergence
at the top, a broad plateau of good values, slow crawl at the bottom.

Deliberately break it once. Set the learning rate to 10 and watch the loss go
to NaN. Knowing what that failure looks like saves an afternoon later.

## Pitfalls

- Comparing optimisers at a single learning rate. Each has its own optimum;
  a comparison without per-optimiser tuning tells you nothing.
- Applying weight decay to biases and normalisation parameters. Convention is
  to exclude them.
- Assuming Adam removes the need to tune. It widens the good range; it does not
  eliminate it.
- Changing two things at once and attributing the result to one of them.

## Further reading

- Kingma & Ba (2014), *Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization*.
- Loshchilov & Hutter (2017), *Decoupled Weight Decay Regularization*.

# Lesson 14 — Convolutions, and why they are a poor fit here: Theory

**ML** · *Stage 2: Supervised deep learning*
## The idea

A convolution slides a small set of shared weights across the input. That
encodes two assumptions: **locality** (nearby values are related) and
**translation invariance** (a pattern means the same thing wherever it appears).

For photographs both hold. For sudoku the second one is plainly false -- and
the lesson is that a wrong prior can still be useful.

## Why translation invariance is wrong here

Shift a picture of a cat one pixel right and it is still a cat. Shift a sudoku
grid one cell right and it is destroyed: cells move between boxes, and the
puzzle's constraints no longer hold.

Worse, position carries meaning that no amount of local pattern matching
recovers. Cell (0,0) and cell (4,4) sit in different boxes with different
peers. A purely convolutional model must infer box membership from position,
which it can only do if position is somehow available to it.

## Why convolutions help anyway

Two reasons, and neither is the translation prior:

1. **Weight sharing is regularisation.** Far fewer parameters than a dense
   layer over 81 cells, so less overfitting on a fixed budget.
2. **Locality is genuinely present.** A 3x3 kernel aligned to box boundaries
   covers exactly one box. The 3x3 grid structure and the 3x3 kernel are a
   happy coincidence worth exploiting -- test whether aligning kernels to box
   boundaries beats the default alignment.

## Receptive fields

Stacked 3x3 convolutions with stride 1 grow the receptive field by 2 per layer:
3, 5, 7, 9. So four layers are needed before a cell can see the whole grid.

Contrast that with the constraint graph from Lesson 02, whose **diameter is 2**
-- every cell is at most two hops from any other. A graph or attention layer
reaches the whole board in two steps; convolution needs four layers to cover a
distance the problem's own structure spans in two. That gap is the argument for
Lessons 15 and 16.

## Pitfalls

- **Never pool.** Pooling discards cell identity, and in sudoku the identity of
  a cell is the entire point. Keep the spatial dimensions at 9x9 throughout.
- Padding choices matter more than usual: `padding=1` on a 3x3 preserves 9x9,
  and zero padding introduces a fake border that the model must learn to ignore.
- Confusing "the CNN beat the MLP" with "the convolutional prior is correct".
  It beat the MLP on parameters and locality, not on translation invariance.

## Further reading

- Dumoulin & Visin (2016), *A guide to convolution arithmetic for deep
  learning*, for receptive fields and padding.

# Lesson 15 — Architectures that know about units: Theory

**ML** · *Stage 2: Supervised deep learning*
## The idea

Rather than hoping a network discovers that rows, columns and boxes matter, put
that structure directly into the layer. This is **inductive bias**: knowledge
encoded in the architecture rather than learned from data.

The operation is pool-and-broadcast. For each of the 27 units, summarise its
nine cells, then send that summary back to every cell in the unit.

## Formally

Let `h_i` be the hidden state of cell `i`. For each unit `U`, compute an
aggregate with a **permutation-invariant** function -- sum, mean or max, so that
reordering cells within the unit does not change the result:

    a_U = aggregate({ h_j : j in U })

Then update each cell from its own state and the three units it belongs to:

    h_i <- f(h_i, a_row(i), a_col(i), a_box(i))

Because `f` is shared across all cells and the aggregate is shared across all
27 units, the layer is **equivariant** to permutations within a unit: permuting
cells inside a row permutes the outputs the same way. That is exactly the
symmetry an all-different constraint has, and it means the layer cannot waste
capacity learning that row 3 behaves like row 7.

This is message passing on a hypergraph, where each unit is a hyperedge over
nine cells. Lesson 22 does the same thing on the ordinary graph, where each
edge joins two cells.

## Why it matters here

It isolates a question worth being able to answer generally: **how much of a
model's performance comes from architecture, and how much from capacity?**

Compare against the CNN at matched parameter count, not matched layer count. If
the unit-aware model wins at equal parameters, the bias is doing real work. If
it only wins when it is also bigger, you have learned something less
interesting.

Cells still need individual identity -- pooling alone makes every cell in a row
interchangeable. Keep a per-cell positional component in `h_i`.

## Pitfalls

- Aggregating with something order-dependent (concatenation, an RNN over the
  nine cells). That breaks the symmetry you are trying to encode.
- Comparing at unequal parameter counts and declaring architectural victory.
- Dropping positional information entirely and wondering why the model cannot
  distinguish cells within a unit.

## Further reading

- Zaheer et al. (2017), *Deep Sets*, for why sum/mean aggregation is the
  general form of a permutation-invariant function.

# Lesson 16 — Transformers over 81 tokens: Theory

**ML** · *Stage 2: Supervised deep learning*
## The idea

Treat the grid as a sequence of 81 tokens and let attention decide which cells
are relevant to which. Where Lesson 15 imposed the unit structure, here the
model can discover it -- and you can check whether it does.

## Formally

Scaled dot-product attention:

    Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d_k)) V

Each token emits a query, a key and a value. The query-key dot products give a
weight over all tokens; the output is the weighted sum of values. The
`sqrt(d_k)` divisor keeps the dot products from growing with dimension and
saturating the softmax.

Multi-head attention runs several of these in parallel with different
projections, so one head can attend along rows while another attends within
boxes.

**Positional encoding is not optional.** Self-attention is permutation
equivariant: shuffle the tokens and the outputs shuffle identically. Without
position, all 81 cells are interchangeable and the model cannot represent the
board at all. For a grid, either a learned per-cell embedding (81 vectors) or
the sum of a row embedding, a column embedding and a box embedding works. The
second is more structured and usually needs less data.

## Structure imposed vs structure learned

At 81 tokens, attention is `81 x 81` -- trivially cheap, so none of the
efficiency machinery matters here. That frees you to run the experiment that
does matter: **mask attention to peers only** and compare against unmasked.

- If masking wins, the structural prior is worth more than the flexibility.
- If unmasked wins, the model found something you did not encode.

Then visualise the attention maps. A well-trained unmasked model tends to
rediscover rows, columns and boxes, which is a genuinely satisfying thing to see
in a heatmap.

Depth matters more than width here. Palm, Paquet and Winther (2018) reported
that a recurrent relational network solving sudoku needed many message-passing
steps -- iterated reasoning, not a wider single step, is what closes hard
puzzles.

## Pitfalls

- Omitting positional encoding. The model will train and produce nonsense.
- Too few layers. One attention layer is one hop of reasoning.
- Reading attention maps as explanations. They show where information flowed,
  not why -- a well-documented caveat in the interpretability literature.

## Further reading

- Vaswani et al. (2017), *Attention Is All You Need*.
- Palm, Paquet & Winther (2018), *Recurrent Relational Networks*.

# Lesson 17 — Iterative decoding: the confidence trick: Theory

**ML** · *Stage 2: Supervised deep learning*
## The idea

This is the pivotal lesson in the repo.

Ask a network for all 81 cells at once and it produces 81 independent
probability distributions. Nothing in that output can express "these answers
must be consistent with each other". The model can be individually plausible
about every cell and jointly wrong.

Then change one thing: fill only the cell it is most confident about, feed the
updated board back in, and run it again. Repeat until full. The same weights,
with no retraining, get dramatically better.

## Formally

Single-shot decoding models the joint distribution as a product of independents:

    p(y | x) ~= prod_i p(y_i | x)

That factorisation cannot represent constraints between cells. Iterative
decoding instead builds a chain of conditionals:

    p(y | x) = p(y_(1) | x) * p(y_(2) | x, y_(1)) * ...

which is autoregressive decoding with a **learned order** -- most confident
first -- rather than a fixed one. Each step conditions on strictly more
information than the last, so the hard cells are decided when the board is
already mostly filled and the constraints have narrowed the possibilities.

## The connection worth noticing

Look at what this procedure actually does: it finds the cell whose answer is
most determined, commits it, propagates the consequence by re-running, and
repeats.

That is **naked singles** with a learned confidence function in place of a
proof. The neural network has been coaxed into performing constraint
propagation, using the same schedule the classical solver uses, without ever
being told the rules.

Which raises the honest question the lesson ends on: if the algorithm is doing
the reasoning and the network is only supplying an ordering heuristic, how much
of the credit belongs to the model? Stage 3 takes that question seriously.

## Cost

Roughly 50 forward passes instead of one for a 30-clue puzzle. On a GPU with
batched puzzles this is usually still fast, but it is a real trade -- and worth
measuring rather than assuming.

## Pitfalls

- Re-using the first forward pass instead of re-running the model. Then you
  have merely sorted the original predictions, and accuracy barely moves.
- Picking the most confident cell overall rather than the most confident
  *empty* cell.
- Error compounding. One confidently wrong fill poisons everything after it.
  The mitigation is Stage 4's lesson: verify with the solver and revisit.

## Further reading

- Compare with beam search and with masked-language-model decoding orders; the
  same "easiest first" intuition recurs across domains.

# Lesson 18 — Loss design and masking: Theory

**ML** · *Stage 2: Supervised deep learning*
## The idea

The loss is the only thing the model is actually optimising. If it does not
match what you care about, everything downstream is negotiation with the wrong
objective.

## Formally

Per cell, a 9-way cross-entropy over the softmax of the logits:

    loss_i = -log p_i(y_i)

Average over the cells you asked the model to predict -- **the empty ones**.
Givens are inputs, not predictions. Including them:

- inflates the reported accuracy for free (a 40-clue puzzle is 49% given), and
- spends capacity teaching the model to copy its own input.

Mask them out of both the loss and the metric.

## Class balance

A completed sudoku contains each digit exactly nine times, so the *digit*
distribution is balanced by construction. The imbalance that matters here is
across **difficulty**: if most puzzles in a batch are easy, the gradient is
dominated by cells that propagation would have solved anyway. Weighting by clue
count is worth trying, and worth measuring rather than assuming.

## Auxiliary constraint loss

You can push the model towards legal outputs without a hard constraint. For
unit `U` and digit `d`, a valid solution has exactly one cell in `U` holding
`d`, so the predicted probabilities should sum to one:

    penalty = sum_U sum_d ( 1 - sum_{i in U} p_i(d) )^2

This is differentiable and cheap. It does not guarantee validity -- it only
rewards outputs that look like they satisfy the constraint in expectation.
Whether it helps grid accuracy is an empirical question, and a good one.

## The result you should expect to find

At some point you will make a change that lowers the loss and does **not**
improve grid accuracy, or even hurts it. That is not a bug. Cross-entropy
rewards being confidently right on easy cells, and grid accuracy is decided
entirely by the hard ones. Finding one concrete instance of this divergence and
understanding it is the point of the lesson.

## Pitfalls

- Scoring givens. The most common way to report a flattering number.
- Tuning against the loss curve rather than the metric you care about.
- Adding an auxiliary loss with an untuned weight and concluding it "does not
  work". Sweep the weight.

## Further reading

- Wang et al. (2019), *SATNet*, for the more ambitious version of this idea:
  a differentiable satisfiability layer rather than a soft penalty.

# Lesson 19 — Calibration and failure analysis: Theory

**ML** · *Stage 2: Supervised deep learning*
## The idea

A model's headline number tells you very little. Where it fails, and whether
its confidence means anything, tell you what to do next.

Calibration matters here more than usual, because Lesson 17's decoder **uses
confidence to choose what to fill first**. If confidence is not meaningful, the
ordering is arbitrary and the whole procedure degrades.

## Formally

A model is **calibrated** if, among predictions made with confidence `p`, a
fraction `p` are correct. Plot it: bin predictions by confidence, and for each
bin plot mean confidence against observed accuracy. Perfect calibration is the
diagonal. This is a **reliability diagram**.

Summarise the gap as **expected calibration error**:

    ECE = sum_b (n_b / N) * | accuracy(b) - confidence(b) |

Modern neural networks are typically **over-confident** -- the curve sits below
the diagonal (Guo et al., 2017). More capacity and longer training generally
make this worse, even as accuracy improves.

**Temperature scaling** is the standard fix: divide the logits by a single
scalar `T` fitted on validation data.

    p = softmax(z / T)

`T > 1` softens the distribution. It is the simplest possible post-hoc method
and usually most of the available benefit.

## The specific insight for this repo

Temperature scaling does not change which class has the highest probability, so
**single-shot accuracy is completely unaffected**.

But it does change the *relative ordering of confidence across cells* -- and
that ordering is exactly what iterative decoding consumes. So calibration can
change grid accuracy without changing the argmax anywhere. That is a sharp,
testable prediction, and one worth verifying yourself.

## Stratified failure analysis

Aggregate accuracy hides the shape of the failure. Use
`metrics.by_clue_count` and find the clue count where grid accuracy collapses.
Every model in this stage has one. Naming it precisely -- "solid above 30
clues, falls off a cliff below 26" -- is far more useful than a single number,
and it is the honest way to compare two models.

## Pitfalls

- Fitting the temperature on the test set. It is a fitted parameter; it needs
  its own held-out data.
- Assuming better calibration means better accuracy. It usually does not, and
  here that is exactly the point.
- Reporting one aggregate number for a mixed-difficulty test set. You are
  reporting the mix as much as the model.

## Further reading

- Guo et al. (2017), *On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks*.

# Lesson 20 — The solver as an environment: Theory

**Engineering** · *Stage 3: Learned search*
## The idea

Before you can learn a decision, the decision has to be observable, swappable
and measurable. That plumbing is most of the work in any applied
imitation-learning or reinforcement-learning project, and it is worth doing
carefully before any model exists.

The solver already exposes the two decisions it makes:

    select_var(domains, stats) -> int      which cell to branch on
    order_values(domains, cell) -> list    which digits to try, in what order

Anything callable can stand in. A learned policy drops into the same slot as
MRV, and the search code does not change.

## State featurisation

The hard design question is what the policy sees. A reasonable state is derived
entirely from the current domains:

- candidate count per cell (the raw material MRV uses)
- how many cells are already decided
- current search depth
- per-cell aggregates over its peers -- how constrained its neighbourhood is

Two properties matter:

**No leakage.** Features must be computable during search. Anything derived
from the solution -- including "is this the value in the answer" -- makes
training scores meaningless.

**Symmetry.** The features should respect the same symmetries the problem has
(Lesson 10). A feature keyed on raw cell index invites the model to memorise
positions rather than learn a policy.

## Measurement

Node count is the objective, and it is why `SearchStats` exists. Wall-clock
time confounds the policy's quality with how slow a Python forward pass is, and
in Stage 3 that confound is enormous.

Sanity-check the harness before trusting it: a **random** variable ordering
should be markedly worse than MRV. If it is not, the instrumentation is wrong
or your puzzles are too easy to discriminate between policies -- generate
harder ones.

## Pitfalls

- Building features that depend on the solution.
- Collecting traces from easy puzzles only, then deploying on hard ones. The
  state distribution differs, which is Lesson 21's problem in advance.
- Measuring seconds.
- Forgetting that `record=True` costs memory on long searches.

## Further reading

- Russell & Norvig chapter 6.3 for the heuristics you are trying to beat.

# Lesson 21 — Imitation learning for variable ordering: Theory

**ML** · *Stage 3: Learned search*
## The idea

The cheapest way to learn a policy is to copy one that already works.
**Behavioural cloning** turns control into supervised learning: collect
`(state, expert action)` pairs, fit a classifier, deploy it as the policy.

Here the expert is MRV, and the immediate consequence is worth stating plainly:
**perfect imitation can only tie.** A student that reproduces the teacher
exactly explores exactly the same tree. Cloning is a way to *match* a heuristic,
not to beat it.

That makes it a good first experiment and a bad final one.

## Distribution shift

The subtler problem is that training and deployment differ. Traces are
collected while the *expert* drives, so they cover the states MRV visits. Once
the student drives, its own small errors take it into states the expert never
demonstrated, where it has no training signal -- and errors compound.

This is the classic failure of behavioural cloning. **DAgger** (Ross, Gordon &
Bagnell, 2011) fixes it by iterating: run the student, ask the expert what it
would have done in the states the student actually reached, add those to the
dataset, retrain.

## How to actually beat the teacher

You need a target better than "what MRV did". The available one is outcome:
for a given state, which choice actually led to fewer nodes? Obtaining that
label means rolling out alternatives and measuring, which is expensive but
entirely feasible offline given a fast solver -- and you have one.

At that point you have stopped imitating and started doing search-based policy
improvement, which is the honest bridge into Lesson 23.

## Measuring it properly

Report three node counts on the same puzzles: random ordering, learned policy,
true MRV. Imitation accuracy -- "the model picks MRV's cell 87% of the time" --
is a training diagnostic, not a result. The result is nodes.

And keep the cost asymmetry in view: MRV is a loop over 81 integers. A neural
network forward pass at every node is thousands of times more expensive. Nodes
saved is the interesting number; wall clock is the sobering one.

## Pitfalls

- Reporting imitation accuracy as if it were performance.
- Training on expert-visited states only and being surprised by deployment.
- Concluding the approach failed when the model ties MRV. Tying is the ceiling
  of what cloning can do.

## Further reading

- Ross, Gordon & Bagnell (2011), *A Reduction of Imitation Learning and
  Structured Prediction to No-Regret Online Learning* (DAgger).

# Lesson 22 — Graph neural networks on the constraint graph: Theory

**ML** · *Stage 3: Learned search*
## The idea

Lesson 02 established that sudoku is a graph. A graph neural network computes
on that graph directly: each cell holds a vector, and cells repeatedly exchange
messages with their peers.

This is the most natural architecture for the problem, because the computation
graph *is* the constraint graph.

## Formally

One round of message passing:

    m_i = AGGREGATE({ MESSAGE(h_i, h_j) : j in peers(i) })
    h_i <- UPDATE(h_i, m_i)

`AGGREGATE` must be permutation invariant -- sum, mean or max -- because a
cell's 20 peers have no meaningful order. `MESSAGE` and `UPDATE` are small
shared MLPs, so the parameter count is independent of graph size.

Node features should carry what the solver knows: the current digit if
assigned, and the candidate set as a 9-bit vector if not.

## Depth, diameter and over-smoothing

The constraint graph has **diameter 2**: two rounds suffice for information to
reach every cell from every other. It is tempting to conclude two rounds are
enough. They are not -- reaching is not the same as reasoning. Constraint
propagation is iterative, and each round of message passing performs roughly
one round of inference. Palm et al. (2018) used tens of steps.

But depth has a cost. **Over-smoothing** is the tendency of repeated
neighbourhood averaging to make all node representations converge toward each
other, at which point the network can no longer tell cells apart. On a
20-regular graph with diameter 2, every node sees almost the whole graph after
two hops, so smoothing sets in fast.

The standard mitigations are residual connections and a gated update -- using a
GRU cell as `UPDATE` rather than a plain MLP, so each node controls how much of
the incoming message it absorbs. That is precisely what recurrent relational
networks do, and it is why they can run many steps without collapsing.

## Why implement it by hand

`EDGES` is a list of 810 pairs. Message passing over it is a gather, an MLP, a
scatter-add and an update -- forty lines. Writing that once teaches more than
learning a library's API, and it makes the over-smoothing experiment easy to
instrument.

## Pitfalls

- Going deep without residual or gated updates, then blaming the architecture.
- Aggregating with concatenation, which imposes a false ordering on peers.
- Omitting candidate sets from node features, leaving the model to rediscover
  propagation from scratch.

## Further reading

- Gilmer et al. (2017), *Neural Message Passing for Quantum Chemistry*.
- Palm, Paquet & Winther (2018), *Recurrent Relational Networks*.

# Lesson 23 — Reinforcement learning for heuristic selection: Theory

**ML** · *Stage 3: Learned search*
## The idea

Reinforcement learning fits problems where you take a sequence of actions and
only learn much later whether they were any good. Search is exactly that shape:
you make hundreds of branching decisions and find out the cost -- total nodes --
only at the end.

It is also, usually, the wrong first tool. This lesson is partly about learning
when *not* to reach for it.

## The credit assignment problem

A search that explores 300 nodes made hundreds of decisions. One early mistake
may account for the entire blow-up while every later decision was fine.
Distributing that single scalar of feedback across the decisions that caused it
is the central difficulty, and it is why RL is sample-hungry.

## Start with a bandit

Before full RL, try a **contextual bandit**: at each node, choose among a small
set of hand-written heuristics (MRV, degree, random, LCV-weighted) based on
features of the current state, and get immediate feedback. No long-horizon
credit assignment, far less variance, often most of the available benefit.

Only if that plateaus is the full formulation worth the trouble.

## REINFORCE

The classic policy-gradient estimator (Williams, 1992):

    grad J = E[ grad log pi(a | s) * (R - b) ]

Raise the log-probability of actions that did better than a baseline `b`, lower
it for those that did worse. Without a baseline the variance is enormous; the
running mean reward is the simplest choice that works.

**Reward shaping matters more than the algorithm here.** Node counts are
heavy-tailed (Lesson 08), so raw `-nodes` is dominated by rare catastrophes.
Something like `-log(nodes)`, or the ratio to a reference solver's node count on
the same puzzle, gives a far better-behaved signal.

## Report it honestly

There is a real chance MRV wins. MRV is a strong, nearly free heuristic refined
over decades, and a learned policy pays a forward pass at every node. If your
agent loses, say so and explain the cost model. A negative result that is
correctly measured is worth more than a positive one that is not.

## Pitfalls

- Skipping the bandit and going straight to policy gradients.
- Unnormalised, heavy-tailed rewards.
- No baseline, then blaming the algorithm for the variance.
- Comparing on puzzles too easy for search quality to matter.

## Further reading

- Williams (1992), *Simple statistical gradient-following algorithms*.
- Sutton & Barto, *Reinforcement Learning*, chapters 13 and 2.

# Lesson 24 — The hybrid solver: Theory

**ML** · *Stage 3: Learned search*
## The idea

Put the two halves together: symbolic search for correctness, a learned policy
for speed. This is the payoff of Stage 3, and it illustrates the property that
makes neurosymbolic systems attractive.

**The model is allowed to be wrong.** A learned heuristic that makes a bad
choice costs you extra nodes; it cannot cost you a wrong answer, because the
search still verifies every assignment against the real constraints. Compare
that with Stage 2, where a wrong prediction is simply a wrong answer.

That asymmetry is the general lesson: guiding a sound procedure is a much safer
place to put a learned component than generating the answer outright.

## The cost model

Node reduction is not free. At each node you pay one forward pass. Guidance is
worth it only when

    nodes_saved * time_per_node > nodes_visited * time_per_inference

For easy puzzles, propagation already solves everything and `nodes_saved` is
near zero, so guidance is pure overhead. For hard instances where search
explodes, the arithmetic can flip decisively.

Mitigations worth trying:

- Call the model only above a depth or domain-size threshold, falling back to
  MRV elsewhere.
- Batch inference across branches.
- Distil the policy into something tiny (Lesson 40) -- a small MLP or even a
  learned linear scoring function over the same features.

## What to produce

One table, three rows, same puzzles, same seeds:

| approach | correct | median nodes | median ms |
|---|---|---|---|
| pure symbolic (MRV) | always | | |
| pure neural (Stage 2, iterative) | sometimes | n/a | |
| hybrid | always | | |

The interesting cell is the neural row's "sometimes". That column is the whole
argument for keeping the solver in the loop.

## Pitfalls

- Reporting nodes without time, or time without nodes. Both mislead alone.
- Evaluating on puzzle difficulties where search is not the bottleneck.
- Quietly changing the propagation strength between arms of the comparison.

## Further reading

- The learning-to-branch literature in mixed-integer programming attacks
  exactly this problem at industrial scale; Khalil et al. (2016) is a
  reasonable entry point.

# Lesson 25 — Finding the grid in a photograph: Theory

**Computer Vision** · *Stage 4: Perception*
## The idea

Getting a puzzle out of a photograph is a geometry problem before it is a
recognition problem. Classical computer vision solves it well, with no training
data, and this lesson is a useful corrective to reaching for a network first.

## The pipeline

**Greyscale, then adaptive threshold.** A global threshold fails the moment
lighting is uneven -- a shadow across one corner turns half the grid black.
Adaptive thresholding computes a threshold per neighbourhood, so local contrast
is what matters. Otsu's method is a good global choice when lighting *is* even,
and a good thing to compare against to see the difference.

**Contours.** Find connected boundaries in the binary image, then take the
largest by area whose polygonal approximation has four sides. `approxPolyDP`
simplifies a contour to its corners; the tolerance is a parameter worth
understanding rather than copying.

**Perspective transform.** A photograph of a plane taken at an angle is related
to the true plane by a **homography**: a 3x3 matrix with 8 degrees of freedom,
determined exactly by four point correspondences. Map the four detected corners
to the corners of a square and warp.

**Corner ordering matters.** The four points come back in arbitrary order, and
mapping them wrongly gives a rotated or mirrored board that then produces a
confidently wrong puzzle. The usual trick: the top-left corner minimises `x+y`,
bottom-right maximises it, and the other two are separated by the sign of
`x-y`.

## Why not learn this

The task is exactly specified, geometric, and has a closed-form solution. A
learned detector would need labelled data, would be slower, and would fail in
ways that are harder to debug. Use learning where the mapping is genuinely
unknown -- which, in this pipeline, is digit recognition and nothing else.

## Pitfalls

- Assuming the largest contour is the grid. It is often the page, the phone
  screen edge, or a table.
- No failure path. "No grid found" is a legitimate and necessary outcome.
- Warping to a non-square, which distorts digits before classification.
- Tuning thresholds on one photograph.

## Further reading

- Szeliski, *Computer Vision: Algorithms and Applications*, on homographies.
- OpenCV's own tutorials for `adaptiveThreshold`, `findContours`,
  `approxPolyDP` and `warpPerspective`.

# Lesson 26 — Cell extraction and empty detection: Theory

**Computer Vision** · *Stage 4: Perception*
## The idea

With a square, upright grid image, cutting 81 cells is arithmetic. The work is
in the details that decide whether the classifier gets a clean digit or a mess.

## Trimming and centring

Cell boundaries include grid lines. A naive `image[r*h/9:(r+1)*h/9]` leaves dark
lines around every crop, and to a classifier trained on clean digits those look
like strokes. Inset each crop by a few percent, or detect and remove lines
explicitly.

Then **centre the digit**. MNIST digits are size-normalised into a 20x20 box
and centred by centre of mass inside a 28x28 field. Matching that convention at
inference removes a large slice of the domain gap in Lesson 28 for almost no
effort. A digit sitting in the corner of its cell is a different input from the
same digit centred, and the model has only ever seen the latter.

## Empty detection, and why its errors are asymmetric

Deciding "is there a digit here at all" is usually ink density above a
threshold. The two ways to be wrong are not equally bad:

- **A digit read as empty** loses a clue. The puzzle is under-constrained and
  may have many solutions -- you get a plausible but wrong answer.
- **An empty cell read as a digit** adds a false constraint. The puzzle usually
  becomes unsolvable, which is *loud*, and Lesson 30 can act on it.

Prefer the loud failure. It is better to be told the pipeline failed than to be
handed a confident wrong grid.

## Pitfalls

- A single global ink threshold across varying lighting.
- Forgetting that the classifier's preprocessing must match its training
  preprocessing exactly -- same normalisation, same scaling, same polarity.
- Not measuring the empty/filled confusion separately from digit accuracy. They
  are different failure modes with different consequences.

## Further reading

- The MNIST website's description of how the digits were normalised and
  centred; it is short, and matching it is worth real accuracy.

# Lesson 27 — Digit classification with MNIST: Theory

**ML** · *Stage 4: Perception*
## The idea

MNIST is 70,000 handwritten digits -- 60,000 train, 10,000 test -- as 28x28
greyscale images. It is the standard first classification dataset, small enough
to train in a minute and rich enough to be non-trivial.

It is cached in `data/raw`, so this lesson works offline.

## What to build

A small convolutional network gets above 99% test accuracy without effort:
two or three conv layers with ReLU and max pooling, then a linear head. This is
one of the few places in the repo where pooling is correct -- for an image
classifier, translation tolerance is the right prior, unlike the sudoku grid in
Lesson 14.

**Drop class 0.** Sudoku has no zero, so nine classes rather than ten. The
model then cannot make a mistake you would have to filter out anyway, and the
comparison is worth running: does removing a class help, hurt, or do nothing?

## Read the confusion matrix

Accuracy is one number; the confusion matrix is the diagnosis. Expect the
errors to concentrate in a few predictable pairs -- 4 against 9, 3 against 5
against 8, 1 against 7 -- because those digits genuinely share strokes when
written quickly.

This matters downstream. If your classifier's most likely confusion is 1 for 7,
then Lesson 30's repair step should try 7 when 1 fails, rather than searching
blindly.

## The number that should worry you

99% on MNIST sounds finished. It is not. A 30-clue puzzle needs all 30 digits
right, and `0.99^30` is about 0.74 -- roughly one puzzle in four fails outright.
Per-item accuracy and per-task accuracy are very different quantities whenever a
task needs many items correct at once, and that gap is Lesson 30's subject.

## Pitfalls

- Normalising differently at training and inference.
- Reporting test accuracy and stopping. It will not survive contact with real
  cell crops (Lesson 28).
- Using the test set to choose hyperparameters.

## Further reading

- LeCun et al. (1998), *Gradient-based learning applied to document
  recognition* -- the original LeNet paper.

# Lesson 28 — The domain gap: Theory

**ML** · *Stage 4: Perception*
## The idea

Your classifier scores over 99% on MNIST. Run it on digits cut from a real
sudoku photograph and it may fall to something dismal.

Nothing is broken. The model was trained on one distribution and deployed on
another, and it never had any reason to generalise across the difference. This
is **distribution shift**, and specifically **covariate shift**: the inputs
changed, the labels mean the same thing.

## What actually differs

Printed sudoku digits differ from MNIST handwriting in ways that are obvious
once listed and invisible until you look:

- **Stroke weight.** Print is thin and uniform; MNIST strokes are thick, and
  the model may key on that.
- **Anti-aliasing.** Print has smooth grey edges; MNIST is heavily binarised.
- **Font.** A printed 1 often has a serif and a base; a handwritten 1 is a
  stroke. A printed 7 rarely has the crossbar many handwritten 7s do.
- **Centring and scale.** Handled in Lesson 26, and the single cheapest fix.
- **Polarity and contrast.** Dark-on-light versus light-on-dark will destroy
  accuracy outright if you get it backwards.

## Diagnosing rather than guessing

Do not jump to fine-tuning. Look at the misclassified crops next to MNIST
examples of the same digit and identify which difference is responsible. Often
one preprocessing change -- matching stroke thickness by dilation, or matching
the centring convention -- recovers most of the gap for free, and that is a
much better outcome than a fine-tuned model whose failure you never understood.

Then fine-tune on printed digits, or train on synthetic ones (Lesson 29), and
re-measure.

## The lesson in one sentence

Benchmark accuracy is a statement about a dataset, not about a model's ability
to do a job.

## Pitfalls

- Reporting MNIST accuracy as if it predicted deployed accuracy.
- Fine-tuning on the same images you evaluate on.
- Fixing the symptom with more capacity rather than the cause with better
  preprocessing.

## Further reading

- Quinonero-Candela et al. (2009), *Dataset Shift in Machine Learning*, for the
  taxonomy of shifts.

# Lesson 29 — Synthetic training data: Theory

**Computer Vision** · *Stage 4: Perception*
## The idea

You need labelled images of printed sudoku digits. Rather than photograph and
annotate hundreds of puzzles, render them -- and get perfect labels for free.

This is the same move as the solver-as-oracle idea in `DESIGN.md`, applied to
perception: generate the data, and the labels come with it by construction.

## Domain randomisation

The naive version produces clean, identical renders, and a model trained on
them fails on real photographs -- the synthetic distribution is far narrower
than reality.

**Domain randomisation** (Tobin et al., 2017) inverts the problem. Rather than
trying to make the synthetic data realistic, vary it so aggressively that real
photographs look like just another sample from the training distribution. Vary:

- font family, weight and size, using whatever the system provides
- position jitter and slight rotation within the cell
- stroke thickness, via dilation or erosion
- blur, sensor noise, JPEG artefacts
- lighting gradients and shadows across the grid
- perspective, applied before cropping, so cells are subtly non-square
- grid line thickness, and whether lines intrude into the crop

Randomise more than feels reasonable. Under-randomising is the usual failure.

## Evaluating honestly

The metric that matters is **train on synthetic, test on real**. Keep a small
set of genuine photographs purely for evaluation, and never train on it. A
synthetic-to-synthetic score is close to meaningless: you are measuring whether
the model can invert your renderer.

## Why this is worth the effort

Beyond accuracy, it makes the pipeline reproducible and offline. Anyone can
regenerate the dataset from a seed, and there is no photograph collection to
lose or distribute.

## Pitfalls

- Synthetic data that is too clean, which produces a model that is confident
  and wrong on real input.
- Validating on synthetic data only.
- Randomising parameters that do not vary in reality, wasting capacity, while
  leaving a real source of variation fixed.

## Further reading

- Tobin et al. (2017), *Domain Randomization for Transferring Deep Neural
  Networks from Simulation to the Real World*.

# Lesson 30 — Photo to solution, end to end: Theory

**ML** · *Stage 4: Perception*
## The idea

Chain the pieces -- photograph, grid detection, cell extraction, digit
classification, solver -- and measure end to end. The result will be much worse
than any individual stage, and the arithmetic that explains why is the most
useful thing in this lesson.

Then fix it, using the solver as a critic. That repair step is the whole thesis
of this repo in one procedure.

## Error propagation

A puzzle succeeds only if **every** clue is read correctly. With per-digit
accuracy `p` and `k` clues:

    P(puzzle correct) = p^k

At 99% per digit and 30 clues, `0.99^30 ~= 0.74`. At 95%, it is `0.21`. A stage
that looks excellent in isolation is decisive in the aggregate, and this is
why per-item metrics mislead whenever a task requires many items at once.

## Constraint-guided correction

The classical solver is not just the last stage; it is a **verifier**. It can
tell you something the classifier cannot: that the grid you produced is
impossible.

That gives a repair loop:

1. Run the solver on the recognised grid.
2. If it has exactly one solution, you are done.
3. If it has none, at least one digit is wrong. Rank the recognised cells by
   classifier confidence, take the least confident, and try its second-best
   digit. Re-solve.
4. Widen to the two or three least confident cells if needed, and stop after a
   bounded number of attempts.

The cases interact usefully with Lesson 26: a hallucinated digit usually makes
the puzzle unsolvable, which this loop catches. A *missed* digit makes it
under-constrained, which shows up as multiple solutions -- `count_solutions`
detects that just as well.

The repair works because the two systems fail differently. The classifier is
uncertain about glyphs and knows nothing about sudoku; the solver knows the
rules exactly and nothing about images. Each covers the other's blind spot.

## Report both numbers

End-to-end success rate before repair, and after. The gap is the value of
having a sound reasoner in the loop, measured on your own pipeline -- and it is
the number worth quoting if you ever explain this project to anyone.

## Pitfalls

- Trying every digit in every cell. Rank by confidence and bound the search.
- Forgetting the multiple-solutions case.
- Not logging which stage failed, leaving end-to-end accuracy undiagnosable.

## Further reading

- Revisit Lesson 24. This is the same neurosymbolic pattern -- a learned
  component proposing, a sound one verifying -- in a different domain.

# Lesson 31 — What makes a puzzle hard?: Theory

**Classical AI** · *Stage 5: Difficulty and generation*
## The idea

"Hard" is not a property of a puzzle. It is a relationship between a puzzle and
a solver -- and human solvers and search algorithms are very different solvers.

This lesson interrogates three proxies and finds where each one lies.

## The three proxies

**Clue count.** The most visible and the weakest. Fewer clues correlates loosely
with difficulty, but the correlation is poor enough to mislead. The puzzle
library in this repo demonstrates it directly: it contains 24-clue puzzles
needing zero search and 30-clue puzzles needing several guesses.

**Search nodes.** How many times the reference solver had to guess. Objective,
cheap, reproducible -- and *specific to your solver's propagation strength*. Add
hidden singles and every node count changes. Add Regin's all-different filter
(Lesson 37) and many puzzles drop to zero nodes. The proxy measures the pair
(puzzle, solver), not the puzzle.

**Technique depth.** Which human solving techniques are needed: naked singles
only, or hidden singles, or naked pairs, X-wing, and so on. This is closest to
what puzzle publishers use and closest to human perception, and it is the most
work to compute -- you need each technique implemented as a separate rule.

## Where they disagree

The interesting exercise is constructing counterexamples:

- A puzzle with **low node count that feels hard**: propagation happens to
  crack it immediately via a chain a human would not spot, but a person scans
  fruitlessly for a while.
- A puzzle with **high node count that feels easy**: the search branches on a
  cell a human would never choose, while an obvious hidden single sits in plain
  view.

Both exist, and finding one of each teaches more than any correlation
coefficient.

## Why it matters here

Everything in Stage 5 is built on whichever proxy you choose, so choosing it
deliberately -- and knowing what it fails to capture -- is the actual content.

what you care about, and the gap between them bounds how good your model can
usefully be.

- Treating node count as intrinsic to the puzzle.

  information is.
