# Lesson 32 — Feature-based difficulty regression: Theory

**ML** · *Stage 5: Difficulty and generation*
## The idea

Before fitting a neural network, fit something simple to hand-made features.
The classical baseline sets the bar, and often it is not beaten.

This lesson is deliberately placed before the deep-learning attempt (Lesson 33)
so the comparison is honest rather than retrospective.

## Feature engineering

Features you can compute cheaply from the puzzle alone:

- clue count
- distribution of clues: per row, per column, per box -- and their variance,
  since evenly spread clues behave differently from clustered ones
- how many digits appear as clues at all, and how often each does
- number of cells solved by naked singles alone
- number solved after adding hidden singles
- candidate-count statistics after propagation: mean, max, and how many cells
  still have 2 candidates
- how many cells remain undecided when propagation reaches its fixpoint

That last group is the strong one, and it is a good illustration of what
feature engineering actually is: you are not inventing information, you are
running a cheap partial solve and handing the model its result.

## Models

Ridge regression gives a linear, interpretable baseline. Gradient-boosted trees
handle non-linearity and interactions and usually win on tabular data of this
shape. Both are in scikit-learn, already installed.

Inspect feature importance and permutation importance. If "cells undecided
after propagation" dominates everything else, that is a finding -- it says
difficulty is mostly "how far does inference get before it stalls", which is
exactly what Lesson 03 plotted.

## Why it matters here

Tabular problems with good features are where classical methods remain
genuinely competitive. Establishing that bar first is what makes Lesson 33's
result meaningful in either direction.

## Pitfalls

- Leaking the target: any feature computed from the node count is the label in
  disguise.
- Evaluating on the training fold; use cross-validation.
- Reporting R-squared without a baseline -- compare against predicting the mean.

## Further reading

- scikit-learn's guide to permutation importance, which is more trustworthy
  than tree-native importances for correlated features.

# Lesson 33 — Learned difficulty from the raw grid: Theory

**ML** · *Stage 5: Difficulty and generation*
## The idea

Give a network the raw grid and let it learn its own features. Then compare it
honestly against Lesson 32's hand-made ones.

The expected outcome is worth stating in advance: **the network may well lose.**
Publishing that result to yourself, clearly, is the point of the lesson.

## Why deep learning is not obviously right here

Deep learning wins where features are hard to specify and data is abundant --
pixels, audio, text. This problem has neither property:

- The dataset is as large as you like, but the *label* is a scalar proxy with
  limited information content per example (Lesson 31).
- The useful features are cheap to compute and easy to name. When a domain
  expert can write down the right features in an afternoon, learned features
  have less room to add value.

You can reuse an encoder from Stage 2 with a regression head, or train from
scratch. Either way the model must learn to do partial constraint propagation
internally to compete with a feature that simply *ran* the propagator.

## Making the comparison fair

- Same train/validation/test split, grouped (Lesson 11).
- Same target and same error metric.
- Tune both. An untuned baseline beaten by a tuned network proves nothing.
- Report the mean-prediction baseline too, so both numbers have a floor.

## If it loses

Say so, and diagnose why. Plausible reasons: not enough signal in a scalar
label, the network rediscovering propagation from scratch when a feature just
called it, or an architecture that cannot represent iterative inference in the
depth given. Any of these is a real, transferable lesson about when to reach
for deep learning.

## If it wins

Look at what it learned. Do saliency or attention maps highlight the regions a
human would call constrained? A win you cannot explain is a weaker result than
a loss you can.

## Pitfalls

- Tuning the network and not the baseline.
- Treating "deep learning should win" as a prior strong enough to keep tuning
  until it does.
- Comparing on different splits.

## Further reading

- Grinsztajn et al. (2022), *Why do tree-based models still outperform deep
  learning on typical tabular data?*

# Lesson 34 — Generating to a target difficulty: Theory

**ML** · *Stage 5: Difficulty and generation*
## The idea

Close the loop: generate puzzles that hit a requested difficulty. This turns a
predictive model into a generative constraint, and it is a nice study in how
much a model has to be right for it to be useful.

## Rejection sampling first

The obvious approach, and a genuinely good baseline:

    repeat: generate a puzzle; score it; keep it if it is in the target band

Its cost is `1 / P(band)`. If "heavy search" puzzles are 5% of what the
generator produces, you need twenty attempts per keeper. Measure that hit rate
before optimising -- for wide bands, rejection sampling is entirely adequate and
requires no model at all.

It gets expensive exactly where it matters: the extreme bands. This repo's own
library is the illustration -- generating anything above "real search" was hard,
because the generator's natural distribution simply does not produce many.

## Guided digging

The better approach uses the difficulty model to steer the *digging* in
Lesson 07. At each removal, prefer the cell whose removal moves predicted
difficulty toward the target. This is hill-climbing over a discrete space with
a learned objective.

The uniqueness constraint still binds -- every candidate removal must keep
exactly one solution -- so the model narrows the search rather than replacing
it. That combination is the recurring pattern in this repo: a learned component
proposing, a sound one checking.

## Evaluating generation

Hit rate is not enough. Check the **distribution**: if you ask for "hard" a
hundred times, does the resulting spread of node counts actually sit in the hard
band, or does it cluster at the easy edge because that is where the generator
finds it cheapest to land? A generator that technically satisfies the
constraint while hugging its boundary is a common and easily-missed failure.

Also check diversity: guided digging can collapse toward a narrow family of
puzzles that happen to score well. Compare against rejection sampling's spread.

## Pitfalls

- Optimising a proxy hard enough to exploit its errors -- the model's mistakes
  become the generator's preferred outputs.
- Dropping the uniqueness check for speed. That corrupts every label downstream.
- Reporting hit rate without distribution or diversity.

## Further reading

- The "reward hacking" literature is the same phenomenon: optimise a learned
  objective hard enough and you find its flaws rather than the intent.

# Lesson 35 — The same machinery on other puzzles: Theory

**Classical AI** · *Stage 6: Beyond sudoku*
## The idea

Everything built so far is sudoku-shaped only by accident. Underneath is a
general constraint satisfaction problem, and pointing the same solver at other
problems proves it -- while forcing the abstraction to be real rather than
aspirational.

## Formally

A CSP is a triple `(X, D, C)`:

- `X` -- variables
- `D` -- a domain of possible values per variable
- `C` -- constraints, each over some subset of variables, saying which
  combinations are allowed

Sudoku: 81 variables, domain `{1..9}`, 27 all-different constraints. Nothing in
AC-3, MRV, backtracking or DLX depends on those specifics.

## The problems worth encoding

**N-queens.** Variables are columns, domains are rows, constraints forbid shared
rows and diagonals. Note the modelling choice: one variable per column already
encodes "one queen per column", so a whole constraint family disappears into the
representation. Good modelling removes constraints.

**Graph colouring.** Variables are vertices, domain is the colours, constraints
are "adjacent vertices differ". Sudoku *is* this problem on the 20-regular graph
from Lesson 02 with nine colours -- which you can verify by feeding your sudoku
graph to your colouring solver and getting the same answers.

**Latin squares.** Sudoku without the box constraint. Useful for isolating how
much of the difficulty the boxes contribute.

**Futoshiki.** Latin square plus inequality constraints between adjacent cells.
This is the one that breaks a sudoku-only solver, because `<` is not
all-different -- propagation must reason about ordering, so `Revise` needs a
genuine constraint interface rather than the special case it has now.

## Why it matters here

The refactor is the lesson. If your solver needs no sudoku-specific code to
handle four problem families, the abstraction was right. If futoshiki forces
you to rewrite propagation, you have learned exactly where the original design
took a shortcut -- which is Lesson 04's decomposition point arriving from a
different direction.

## Pitfalls

- Building a generic interface so abstract it is slow. Keep the bitmask
  representation for finite small domains.
- Encoding n-queens with one variable per square. It works and it is much worse;
  compare the two and see why.

## Further reading

- Russell & Norvig chapter 6 for the general CSP formulation.

# Lesson 36 — SAT encoding: Theory

**Classical AI** · *Stage 6: Beyond sudoku*
## The idea

Reformulate again, this time as boolean satisfiability, and hand the result to
a solver representing decades of engineering. The point is partly the encoding
skill and partly the humility.

## The encoding

Use `x[r][c][d]` meaning "cell (r,c) holds digit d": `9 * 9 * 9 = 729`
variables. The clauses:

- **Cell:** each cell holds at least one digit -- `(x[r][c][1] or ... or
  x[r][c][9])` for every cell.
- **Row:** each digit appears at least once per row.
- **Column:** likewise per column.
- **Box:** likewise per box.
- **Givens:** a unit clause per clue.

"At least one" of each family plus the at-most-one constraints below is enough;
the encoding is famously redundant, and adding the "at most one per cell"
clauses explicitly usually helps solvers despite being logically implied.

## At-most-one encodings

Expressing "at most one of these `n` variables is true" is a small design
problem in itself:

- **Pairwise:** a clause `(not a or not b)` for every pair. `O(n^2)` clauses,
  no new variables. Fine at `n = 9`.
- **Sequential / commander / bitwise:** introduce auxiliary variables to get
  `O(n)` or `O(n log n)` clauses (Sinz, 2005). Necessary at large `n`,
  unnecessary here -- but implementing both and comparing clause counts and
  solve times is a good exercise in why encoding choice matters.

## Why SAT solvers are fast

Modern CDCL solvers do far more than backtracking: they learn clauses from
conflicts, backjump non-chronologically, restart, and use activity-based
branching heuristics. That machinery generalises across problem families in a
way hand-written heuristics do not.

Expect the SAT solver to be competitive or better on hard instances, and to
carry more overhead on trivial ones where propagation alone suffices.

## Pitfalls

- Off-by-one between 1-indexed digits and 0-indexed variables. The most common
  bug here, and it produces a valid-looking wrong grid.
- Forgetting the givens.
- Comparing solve times without counting encoding time.

## Further reading

- Sinz (2005), *Towards an optimal CNF encoding of boolean cardinality
  constraints*.
- Lynce & Ouaknine (2006), *Sudoku as a SAT problem*.

# Lesson 37 — CP-SAT and global constraints: Theory

**Classical AI** · *Stage 6: Beyond sudoku*
## The idea

CP-SAT is a production constraint solver. Modelling sudoku in it takes about
ten lines, and it will beat everything you have written. The interesting part
is *why* -- and the answer connects straight back to Lesson 04.

## The model

    model = cp_model.CpModel()
    x = [[model.NewIntVar(1, 9, f"x{r}{c}") for c in range(9)] for r in range(9)]
    for each row, column, box:
        model.AddAllDifferent(cells)
    for each given:
        model.Add(x[r][c] == value)

That is the whole thing. Declarative: you state the constraints, not the search.

## Global constraints, and the payoff from Lesson 04

`AddAllDifferent` is not sugar for pairwise `!=`. It is a **global constraint**
with a dedicated propagator that reasons about all nine variables jointly --
Regin's algorithm, based on matching in a bipartite variable-value graph, which
achieves generalised arc consistency.

This is precisely the strength Lesson 04 showed you were missing. Where AC-3 on
the binary decomposition could only propagate from singletons, GAC on
all-different can deduce, for example, that if three cells in a unit share only
the candidates `{4,7,9}` between them, no other cell in that unit may take 4, 7
or 9 -- the naked-triple rule, derived rather than hand-coded.

Run CP-SAT on a puzzle your solver needed many nodes for. Often it needs none.

## What else it brings

Clause learning from the SAT side, portfolio search, presolve that simplifies
the model before search begins, and years of tuning. It is worth reading the
solver log for one hard instance just to see how much is happening.

## The honest conclusion

Your hand-written solver is not going to beat CP-SAT, and that is the correct
result. You built it to understand it. For anything real -- including the
rostering in Lesson 38 -- you should reach for the industrial tool, and now you
know what it is doing.

## Pitfalls

- Concluding your own solver was wasted effort. Lessons 03-06 are why the
  CP-SAT result is intelligible rather than magic.
- Timing without separating model-building from solving.

## Further reading

- Regin (1994), the all-different filtering algorithm.
- The OR-Tools CP-SAT documentation, particularly the section on presolve.

# Lesson 38 — Real constraint problems: Theory

**Classical AI** · *Stage 6: Beyond sudoku*
## The idea

The bridge out of puzzles. Staff rostering, timetabling and scheduling are
constraint satisfaction problems with the same structure as sudoku and two
additions that change everything: **soft constraints** and **explanation**.

## Hard versus soft

A sudoku constraint is hard -- violate it and the grid is invalid. Real problems
have both:

- **Hard:** every shift is covered; nobody works two shifts at once; legally
  required rest between shifts; required qualifications present.
- **Soft:** preferred days off; even distribution of unpopular shifts; shift
  patterns that are humane; minimising overtime cost.

Soft constraints become penalty terms in an objective, so the problem stops
being satisfaction and becomes **optimisation**: find a feasible solution
minimising total penalty. CP-SAT handles this directly -- introduce a violation
variable per soft constraint and minimise a weighted sum.

Choosing those weights is a modelling decision with real consequences for real
people, and it is not a technical question. Making the weights explicit and
reviewable is part of doing this responsibly.

## Explaining infeasibility

This is the genuinely hard part, and the part that decides whether a solver
gets used.

When a roster is infeasible, "no solution" is useless. The user needs to know
*which* requirements conflict: "Tuesday night needs two nurses with paediatric
certification; only one is available who has not already worked the maximum
consecutive nights."

The technique is an **irreducible infeasible subset**: a minimal set of
constraints that is still infeasible together. Find one by removing constraints
until the model becomes feasible, then reporting what was necessary. CP-SAT
supports assumption literals, which make this tractable.

## What transfers, and what does not

Transfers: the CSP formulation, propagation, search, global constraints,
measurement discipline, the value of a sound checker.

Does not: everything that assumed a 9x9 grid, all-different as the only
constraint type, and a single unique solution. Real problems have many
acceptable solutions of differing quality, which is why optimisation replaces
satisfaction.

## Pitfalls

- Modelling soft constraints as hard, producing an infeasible model and an
  unhappy user.
- Weights chosen by whoever wrote the code, never reviewed by anyone affected.
- Returning "infeasible" with no explanation.

## Further reading

- The OR-Tools employee-scheduling examples.
- Any treatment of irreducible infeasible subsets in constraint programming.

# Lesson 39 — Model export and runtime parity: Theory

**Engineering** · *Stage 7: Deployment*
## The idea

A trained model that only runs inside your Python process is not deployed.
ONNX is an interchange format: export the computation graph plus weights, and
run it anywhere there is a runtime -- including a browser (Lesson 41).

## How export works

`torch.onnx.export` **traces**: it runs your model on an example input and
records the operations that actually executed. Two consequences follow directly:

- Control flow that depends on tensor *values* is baked in as whatever happened
  during the trace. An `if x.sum() > 0` becomes one branch, permanently.
- Anything not expressible as an ONNX operator fails at export.

Iterative decoding (Lesson 17) is a Python loop around the model, not part of
it. Export the single forward pass and implement the loop in TypeScript.
That is the right split anyway -- the loop is application logic.

Use `dynamic_axes` to leave the batch dimension free, or you will export a model
that only accepts the batch size you traced with.

## Parity checking

Export is not done when the file is written. It is done when you have asserted:

    torch_out = model(x).detach().numpy()
    onnx_out = session.run(None, {"input": x.numpy()})[0]
    assert np.allclose(torch_out, onnx_out, atol=1e-5)

Exact equality is the wrong test -- operator implementations differ and
floating-point reassociation is legitimate. A tolerance of `1e-5` is generous
for float32; if you cannot meet it, something is genuinely wrong.

Check parity on a *batch* of real inputs, not one hand-made tensor, and compare
the resulting grid accuracy rather than only the logits.

## Deliberately break it once

Use an unsupported operator and read the error. Knowing what an export failure
looks like -- and that the usual fix is rewriting a layer in more common
primitives -- saves an afternoon later.

## Pitfalls

- Exporting in training mode. Call `model.eval()` first, or dropout and batch
  norm behave differently in the exported graph.
- Fixed batch size via missing `dynamic_axes`.
- Assuming parity from a successful export.

## Further reading

- The PyTorch ONNX export documentation, particularly its list of caveats about
  tracing.

# Lesson 40 — Making the model small: Theory

**ML** · *Stage 7: Deployment*
## The idea

The model that trains best is rarely the model you should ship. Deployment cares
about size, latency and memory; training cares about accuracy. Making that
trade deliberately -- with the numbers in front of you -- is the lesson.

## Quantization

Store and compute in int8 rather than float32: four times smaller, and faster
where the hardware supports integer arithmetic.

A quantized tensor approximates floats by an affine map:

    x ~= scale * (q - zero_point)

with `q` an 8-bit integer. `scale` and `zero_point` are chosen per tensor (or
per channel) from the observed range.

- **Post-training quantization** calibrates on a small sample of representative
  data. No retraining. Try this first -- it is often nearly free.
- **Quantization-aware training** simulates the rounding during training so the
  model learns weights robust to it. More work, better accuracy, worth it only
  if PTQ loses too much.

The failure mode to watch for: one layer with a wide activation range dominates
the scale and destroys precision everywhere. Per-channel scales usually fix it.

## Distillation

Train a small **student** to match a large **teacher**'s output distribution
rather than the hard labels (Hinton, Vinyals & Dean, 2015). The soft
probabilities carry more information than a one-hot label -- they say which
wrong answers were plausible, which is a richer signal.

The comparison that matters: distilled student versus the same architecture
trained directly on labels. If distillation does not beat direct training, it
is not earning its complexity.

## Plot the frontier

Size on one axis, grid accuracy on the other, one point per variant. Then pick
a point and justify it. For a browser deployment the constraint is real -- every
megabyte is download time on a phone -- so a model that is 2% worse and 4x
smaller may be the correct ship.

## Pitfalls

- Reporting size and latency without accuracy, or the reverse.
- Calibrating quantization on unrepresentative data.
- Measuring latency without warmup runs; the first inference includes
  initialisation.
- Comparing student to teacher rather than to a directly-trained equal.

## Further reading

- Hinton, Vinyals & Dean (2015), *Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network*.
- Jacob et al. (2018) on integer-arithmetic-only inference.

# Lesson 41 — Running it in the browser: Theory

**ML** · *Stage 7: Deployment*
## The idea

Run the model in the browser. No server, no upload, no inference bill -- and the
user's data never leaves their machine, which for many applications is the
entire argument.

## onnxruntime-web and WASM

onnxruntime-web executes ONNX graphs compiled to WebAssembly, with an optional
WebGPU backend. WASM is a portable binary instruction format that runs at
near-native speed in a sandbox.

Two performance features matter, and both come with conditions:

- **SIMD** gives large speedups on the vector operations that dominate
  inference. Widely supported and generally safe to enable.
- **Threads** need `SharedArrayBuffer`, which browsers gate behind
  **cross-origin isolation** -- the page must be served with
  `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin` and
  `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp`.

**GitHub Pages cannot set response headers**, so threads are unavailable on the
site this repo publishes to. The workaround is a service worker that
synthesises the headers client-side; whether that complexity is worth it is a
judgement call, and for a model this small it probably is not. Ship
single-threaded with SIMD and measure before optimising.

## Loading

The model is likely several megabytes. Do not block first paint on it: render
the UI, let the classical solver handle everything it can, and fetch the model
lazily. Cache it with a service worker (Lesson 50) so the second visit is
instant.

## The neurosymbolic safety net

The most important design decision is that **the browser already has a correct
solver** -- the TypeScript port from Lesson 45. So the model never needs to be
trusted:

1. Model proposes a solution, via iterative decoding.
2. TS solver verifies it.
3. If wrong, fall back to search, which always succeeds.

The user gets a fast answer when the model is right and a correct answer always.
That is the same contract as Lesson 24 and Lesson 30, in a third setting -- and
it is the general reason to keep a sound component beside a learned one.

## Pitfalls

- Blocking page load on the model download.
- Assuming threads are available; feature-detect and degrade.
- Shipping a model whose preprocessing differs from training.
- Testing only on a desktop. Measure on a phone.

## Further reading

- The onnxruntime-web documentation on execution providers and threading.
- MDN on cross-origin isolation and `SharedArrayBuffer`.

lessons.theory:
# Lesson 42 — Reproducibility and experiment tracking: Theory

**Engineering** · *Stage 7: Deployment*
## The idea

The final lesson is retrospective, and it is the habit most likely to outlast
this project: **every number you have quoted should be regenerable from a seed
and a config.**

If you cannot rerun an experiment from three months ago and get the same answer,
you do not have a result, you have an anecdote.

## What reproducibility requires

**Seed everything.** Data generation, augmentation, the train/val/test split,
weight initialisation, batch shuffling, dropout. Each is a separate source of
randomness, and missing one makes runs differ for reasons you cannot see.

**Configuration over constants.** Hyperparameters in a file that is saved with
the run, not literals scattered through a script. Then "what learning rate did
that use?" has an answer.

**A run directory.** One directory per experiment, containing the config, the
seed, the git commit, the metrics, and the model. The commit matters: config
plus code determines the result, and code changes silently.

**Record failures too.** The experiments that did not work are more useful than
the ones that did, because you will otherwise repeat them.

## Honest caveats

Bit-exact reproducibility across machines is harder than it sounds. GPU kernel
non-determinism, library versions, and hardware differences all intrude.
PyTorch offers `torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)`, at some cost in
speed and with some operations unsupported. Aim for reproducible-on-this-machine
first, and record versions (`requirements.lock.txt` already pins them) so the
environment can be rebuilt.

## The final artefact

One table spanning every model you trained: architecture, parameters, decoding
strategy, cell accuracy, grid accuracy, grid accuracy at low clue counts, and
where the config lives. That table is the summary of the whole curriculum, and
building it will show you which comparisons you never actually made fairly.

Then write the paragraph that matters: what worked, what did not, and what
surprised you.

## Pitfalls

- Seeding Python's `random` but not NumPy's or PyTorch's.
- Recording metrics without the config that produced them.
- Assuming determinism you never tested -- rerun something and check.

## Further reading

- The PyTorch reproducibility notes, which are candid about what is not
  achievable.

# Lesson 43 — Rendering the grid in TypeScript: Theory

**Frontend** · *Stage 8: Browser and visualisation*
## The idea

The browser is the right place to watch a solver think. It renders, it is
interactive, it needs no install, and everyone already has one. This stage
builds the interface -- and the first lesson is that a 9x9 grid is a more
interesting layout problem than it looks.

## CSS grid, and the trap

    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: repeat(9, 1fr);
    grid-template-rows: repeat(9, 1fr);
    aspect-ratio: 1;

Both `grid-template-*` lines are load-bearing. Declare only the columns and the
rows are sized by content, so a row of empty cells collapses while rows
containing the heavy box border grow. This repo shipped that bug: measured at
375px wide, one row was 14.4px, most were 38.4px, and two were 40.4px. It was
invisible on a desktop and obvious on a phone.

`1fr` tracks fix it, because a fractional track ignores content entirely.
`aspect-ratio: 1` then keeps the board square as the width changes.

Cells also need `min-width: 0; min-height: 0`. Grid items default to
min-content sizing, so a candidate overlay could otherwise push a track wider
than its share.

## Box boundaries

The 3x3 structure is drawn with borders on specific children via `nth-child`.
Getting the ranges wrong by one row is easy and very visible -- the separators
sit under rows 2 and 5 (0-indexed), which is 1-indexed cells 19-27 and 46-54.
With `box-sizing: border-box` and fixed tracks, those borders do not change
layout.

## Theming and accessibility

Define colours as custom properties on `:root` and override them under
`prefers-color-scheme: dark`. Every colour used by the grid should come from a
token, so a theme change is one block, not a search-and-replace.

Give the container `role="grid"` and cells `role="gridcell"`, manage `tabIndex`
so the board is one tab stop rather than 81, and make sure contrast passes
WCAG AA in both themes -- the default link blue in this repo failed badly on
dark until it was measured.

## Pitfalls

- Content-sized rows. The bug above.
- Pooling the grid into an image mindset -- pixel positions rather than cells.
- Colours defined outside the token system, which then break in one theme.
- Testing only at desktop width.

## Further reading

- MDN's CSS grid guide, particularly the section on `fr` units.

lessons.theory:
# Lesson 44 — Interaction and state: Theory

**Frontend** · *Stage 8: Browser and visualisation*
## The idea

A board you can only look at is a demo. Making it editable raises the questions
every interactive app has to answer: what is the state, what is derived from
it, and what happens when the user does something unexpected.

## State versus derived state

Keep the minimum as state:

- the board (81 digits)
- which cells were given
- the selected cell
- the edit history

Everything else is **derived**, recomputed on render: conflicts, the peers of
the selection, which cells share the selected digit, which digits a pad key
should disable. Deriving is cheap at this size, and it removes the entire class
of bugs where cached state and real state disagree.

## Decisions worth making deliberately

**Selection starts empty.** This repo initialised it to cell 0, so the app
opened with a cell highlighted as if the user had chosen it. `null` is the
honest initial value.

**Givens are immutable.** Guard entry and erase at the model layer, not in the
UI. Both the keyboard and the number pad route through the same
`enterDigit`/`eraseSelected` pair, so the rule cannot be enforced in one and
forgotten in the other.

**Re-selecting the same cell is a no-op**, not a toggle. On touch it is far too
easy to tap twice, and losing your place is worse than doing nothing.

**Undo is over user edits only.** Undoing a solve is meaningless when reloading
the puzzle does the same thing more clearly. A new edit after undoing discards
the redo tail, as in any editor.

## Touch details that matter

`touch-action: manipulation` disables double-tap zoom on the board.
`user-select: none` stops long-press selecting digits as text. Touch targets
should be at least 44px. And any real `<input>` needs a font size of at least
16px, or iOS Safari zooms the page when it receives focus.

## Pitfalls

- Enforcing rules in the view, so a second input path bypasses them.
- Caching derived state and letting it drift.
- Using `click` for selection when `pointerdown` gives a more immediate feel.

## Further reading

- The WAI-ARIA authoring practices for grid widgets, for keyboard conventions.

lessons.theory:
# Lesson 45 — Porting the solver to TypeScript: Theory

**Frontend** · *Stage 8: Browser and visualisation*
## The idea

Port the solver to TypeScript, then prove the two implementations agree. The
port is routine; the proof is the lesson.

**Differential testing** -- running two independent implementations on the same
inputs and comparing -- is one of the most effective bug-finding techniques
available, and it costs almost nothing when you already have a reference.

## What to compare

Not just the solution. A puzzle with a unique solution gives both
implementations the same answer even if their search differs wildly, so
matching solutions proves very little.

Compare **node counts**. Identical node counts mean the two searches made the
same decisions in the same order -- the heuristics, the tie-breaking, and the
propagation all agree. Any divergence points at a specific behavioural
difference, usually an ordering one.

Generate a few hundred puzzles in Python, save `(puzzle, solution, nodes)` as
JSON, and assert all three in TypeScript.

## JavaScript pitfalls that matter here

**Bitwise operators coerce to 32-bit signed integers.** Fine for 9-bit domain
masks, but worth knowing before you assume JavaScript numbers behave like
Python's arbitrary-precision integers.

**There is no `bit_count`.** Python has `int.bit_count()`; JavaScript does not,
so popcount is a loop or a lookup table. `Math.clz32` gives the leading-zero
count, which is how this repo extracts the digit from a singleton mask.

**Typed arrays are not JavaScript arrays.** `Int16Array` gives predictable
memory and fast copies, and `.slice()` on it copies rather than aliasing --
which the search relies on when branching.

**Sorting is lexicographic by default.** `[10, 9].sort()` gives `[10, 9]`.

## Why the port is worth having

It makes the app work with no server, it is the correctness backstop for the
model in Lesson 48, and maintaining two implementations of the same algorithm
in different languages is an unusually good way to discover which parts of your
design were incidental.

## Pitfalls

- Comparing solutions only.
- Porting the code without porting the tests.
- Assuming identical floating-point or integer semantics across languages.

## Further reading

- The general technique is often called differential or back-to-back testing;
  compilers and cryptographic libraries rely on it heavily.

# Lesson 46 — Visualising constraint propagation: Theory

**Frontend** · *Stage 8: Browser and visualisation*
## The idea

Lesson 03 was about inference you had to imagine. This lesson draws it. Showing
the candidate sets shrink turns constraint propagation from an abstraction into
something you can watch happen.

## What to render

Each empty cell displays its remaining candidates as a 3x3 mini-grid, with the
digit in a fixed position so the eye can compare cells without reading. That
fixed layout matters more than it sounds: candidates rendered as a compacted
list ("1 3 8") force you to read each one, while a positional layout lets you
see the pattern.

## Making the inference visible

The interesting part is not the final candidate state, it is the **transition**.
Show:

- which candidates were just eliminated, and by which assignment
- which rule fired -- naked single, hidden single -- in different colours
- for a hidden single, **which unit justified it**, since that is the whole
  content of the deduction

The solver's event log already carries this: `naked-single` and `hidden-single`
events, and the latter records its unit. That is the difference between an
animation and an explanation.

## Find the stall

The most instructive thing to show is where propagation **stops**. Step to the
fixpoint on a hard puzzle and display the remaining candidate sets. The board
is consistent, no rule fires, and nothing is solved -- that is the exact moment
search becomes necessary, and it is much more convincing rendered than
described.

Every cell with two candidates at that point is a place MRV would branch, which
connects directly to Lesson 47.

## Design constraints

Nine candidate digits in a cell that may be 37px wide on a phone is genuinely
tight. Options: show candidates only on larger screens, only for the selected
cell and its peers, or shrink the type and accept it. Measure rather than
guess -- and check the layout does not shift when candidates appear, which is
the trap Lesson 43's fixed tracks exist to prevent.

## Pitfalls

- Rendering the end state only, which teaches nothing about the process.
- Colour as the only channel distinguishing rules; add shape or a label.
- Re-rendering all 81 cells per event on a long trace, which janks.

## Further reading

- Bret Victor's *Learnable Programming* is the standard argument for making
  execution visible rather than described.

# Lesson 47 — Visualising search and backtracking: Theory

**Frontend** · *Stage 8: Browser and visualisation*
## The idea

Animate the search: the guesses, the propagation cascades that follow, the dead
ends, and the walk back up. Done well this makes the value of a heuristic
obvious to someone who has never heard of MRV -- which is a high bar for an
explanation and a good test of whether you understand it.

## Event-log replay

The architectural point is worth stating separately: **do not animate during
the search.** Run the solver to completion, recording an event log, then replay
the log at whatever speed you like.

This separates computation from presentation, and it buys you a great deal:

- the animation speed is independent of solver speed
- you can scrub backwards, which is impossible if you are animating live
- the solver stays synchronous and simple, with no callbacks or yields
- the same log drives a step-by-step explanation later

`SolveEvent` in this repo is that log: `given`, `naked-single`,
`hidden-single`, `branch`, `backtrack`, `contradiction`, `solved`.

## Visual grammar

The single most important distinction is **deduced versus guessed**. A cell
filled by inference is certain; a cell filled by branching is a hypothesis that
may be withdrawn. Give them different colours -- this repo uses blue and orange
-- and make backtracking visibly *undo* the orange ones. Watching a guess get
retracted is what makes backtracking click.

Beyond that, a search tree drawn beside the board, growing as it explores, turns
node count from a number into a shape. Deep narrow trees and bushy shallow ones
look completely different, and the difference is the story.

## The comparison to build toward

Run the same puzzle twice, side by side: first-empty-cell ordering against MRV.
One tree sprawls; the other barely branches. That single image justifies
Lesson 05 better than any table -- and it is the artefact worth keeping.

## Pitfalls

- Animating inside the solver, which entangles the two and makes scrubbing
  impossible.
- Replaying every event at fixed speed; propagation cascades want to be fast
  and branch points want to be slow.
- Logging unconditionally on long searches -- the trace can get large, which is
  why recording is opt-in here.

## Further reading

- The search-tree visualisations in constraint programming tools such as
  CP-Profiler are worth looking at for prior art.

# Lesson 48 — Running your model in the browser: Theory

**ML** · *Stage 8: Browser and visualisation*
## The idea

Load the ONNX model from Stage 7 and run it client-side, with the TypeScript
solver as a correctness backstop. This is where the whole repo converges:
learned perception, symbolic verification, in the user's browser, offline.

## The mechanics

onnxruntime-web loads the model and runs it on a WASM backend. You supply a
tensor, you get logits back. The work on the TypeScript side is marshalling:
building the input tensor in the exact shape and encoding the model was trained
on, and reshaping the output into 81 distributions over 9 digits.

Getting the preprocessing wrong is the most common failure and it fails
quietly -- the model returns plausible nonsense rather than an error. Assert the
tensor shape, and check one known puzzle against the Python output before
trusting anything.

Iterative decoding (Lesson 17) lives here, in TypeScript, not in the exported
graph: run the model, find the most confident empty cell, fill it, repeat.

## The contract that makes this safe

The browser already has a correct solver. So:

1. Model proposes a full solution.
2. Solver checks it: is it complete, consistent, and does it match the puzzle's
   unique solution?
3. If not, fall back to search, which always succeeds.

The user gets a fast answer when the model is right and a correct answer
always. **The model's errors cost latency, not correctness.** That is the same
contract as Lessons 24 and 30, and it is the general reason to keep a sound
component beside a learned one rather than replacing it.

It also gives you a free, honest metric in production: the fallback rate is the
model's real-world accuracy, measured on whatever people actually type in.

## Performance

Measure on a phone, not a laptop. Model download dominates first load, so fetch
it lazily after first paint and cache it (Lesson 50). Threads need
cross-origin isolation, which GitHub Pages cannot provide -- see Lesson 41; ship
single-threaded with SIMD.

## Pitfalls

- Preprocessing drift between training and inference.
- Blocking the UI on a multi-megabyte download.
- Trusting model output without verification, which throws away the one
  guarantee you had.

## Further reading

- The onnxruntime-web docs on tensor creation and execution providers.

# Lesson 49 — Visualising what the model thinks: Theory

**ML** · *Stage 8: Browser and visualisation*
## The idea

Render what the model believes. Confidence and attention are just numbers over
cells, and a 9x9 grid is an ideal canvas for them -- interpretability is far
easier to reason about when the thing you are interpreting has a natural
spatial layout.

## What to draw

**Confidence heatmap.** Colour each empty cell by its maximum predicted
probability. You will usually see high confidence where propagation would have
succeeded anyway and low confidence exactly where search is needed -- which is
itself a finding about what the model learned.

**Per-cell distribution.** For the selected cell, show all nine probabilities as
a bar chart. This is where over-confidence (Lesson 19) becomes visible: a
miscalibrated model puts 0.99 on a digit that is wrong, and you can see it.

**Attention maps.** For the transformer (Lesson 16), pick a cell and shade every
other cell by how much attention it received. A well-trained model tends to
light up the selected cell's row, column and box -- rediscovering the peer
relation from Lesson 02 without being told it.

**Model versus proof.** The most valuable view in this repo: put the model's
prediction next to what constraint propagation *proves*. Cells where they
disagree are exactly where the model is guessing beyond what is derivable, and
those are the interesting cells.

## An honest caveat

Attention weights show where information flowed, not why a decision was made.
This has been argued at length in the interpretability literature, and the
sensible position is that these visualisations are hypothesis-generating tools,
not explanations. Use them to find cases to investigate, not to conclude.

## Diagnosing from the picture

Take a puzzle the model gets wrong and try to explain the failure from the
visualisation alone, before looking at any numbers. If you can, the
visualisation is doing its job. If you cannot, it needs another channel --
which is a more useful finding than adding features speculatively.

## Pitfalls

- Colour scales without a legend, or ones that mislead in dark mode.
- Reading attention as causal explanation.
- Showing only successes.

## Further reading

- Jain & Wallace (2019), *Attention is not Explanation*, and the responses to
  it, for the state of that argument.

# Lesson 50 — Offline-first deployment: Theory

**Engineering** · *Stage 8: Browser and visualisation*
## The idea

Ship the whole thing as a static, installable site that works with no network.
Given that everything already runs client-side, offline is less a feature to
add than a property to stop breaking.

## Static builds

A production build emits hashed asset filenames and an `index.html` referencing
them. Two details matter for this deployment:

**Relative asset paths.** Using a relative base means the same build works from
a GitHub Pages subpath, from a different host, and from a local directory.

**Data must be fetched, not inlined** -- and that means `file://` will not work,
because browsers block `fetch` on file origins. Any static server does; there is
no way around it short of inlining the JSON into the HTML.

## Service workers

A service worker is a script the browser runs between your page and the
network. It can serve requests from a cache, which is what makes offline
possible.

Two strategies, and the choice differs per asset:

- **Cache-first** for the app shell and the model: fixed content, hashed
  filenames, so a cached copy is always correct.
- **Network-first, falling back to cache** for anything that changes.

The classic mistake is caching `index.html` cache-first with a long lifetime.
Users then get an old shell that references assets which no longer exist,
producing a blank page that a refresh does not fix. Version the cache, delete
old caches on activation, and be deliberate about the entry point.

## PWA installation

A web app manifest -- name, icons, `display: standalone`, theme colour -- plus a
service worker makes the site installable. On iOS that is Share, then Add to
Home Screen; the app then launches without browser chrome.

Combined with `localStorage` for the current puzzle and settings, the result
behaves like a native app: launch, resume where you were, work on a plane.

## Testing it honestly

Turn the network off and cold-load the site from the home screen. Not a refresh
with a warm cache -- a genuine cold start with no connectivity. That is the only
test that means anything, and it routinely reveals one asset nobody cached.

## Pitfalls

- A stale `index.html` pinned in cache, the classic PWA failure.
- Forgetting to clean up old caches, so storage grows without bound.
- Assuming iOS supports every PWA capability; it lags, and support varies.
- Never testing an actual cold offline load.

## Further reading

- MDN on service workers and the Cache API.
- Google's PWA checklist, for what "installable" actually requires.
